lessons.plain: A project is a temporary effort with a clear end point that creates something new, like a one-off office move or a new mobile app. Operations is the ongoing, repeating work that keeps an organization running, like a help desk answering calls every day. A program is a group of related projects managed together to reach a bigger goal than any one could reach alone. A portfolio is the wider set of projects, programs and ongoing work an organization chooses to fund and track. Separately, some projects plan every step up front, while others deliver in short rounds and adjust as they learn. Sorting a situation into these boxes helps you pick the right tools and language.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs a help desk every weekday, and separately it is building a new customer portal over the next nine months with a fixed budget. Before reading on, which of these two pieces of work is a project, and why do you think so?
lessons.teach:
A project is temporary work with a defined start and finish that produces a unique result, such as a product, service or upgrade. Temporary means the work has an end point and closes once its goal is met, not that it is short. Operations is ongoing, repeating work that keeps the business running, such as payroll each month or support tickets each day. The two are often confused because both use people and budgets, but operations has no finish line and its outputs are routine.

A program is a group of related projects, and sometimes operations, managed together because their combined benefit is larger than the parts. A portfolio is the broadest view: every project, program and operational activity an organization has chosen to fund, ranked against strategy. Items in a portfolio do not need to be related to one another.

Separately, delivery can be predictive, meaning scope, schedule and cost are planned in detail early and changes go through formal control, or adaptive, meaning work is split into short iterations, requirements are refined as feedback arrives, and the plan is adjusted regularly. Predictive suits well-understood outcomes such as a building; adaptive suits uncertain outcomes such as new software.

Worked example: a bank wants a new mobile app. Step 1: is it temporary and aimed at a unique result? Yes, so it is a project. Step 2: does it share goals with a branch renovation and a fraud-detection project under a digital transformation banner? Yes, so it sits inside a program. Step 3: are requirements stable, regulated and tied to a fixed deadline? If so, choose predictive; if the requirements are unclear, choose adaptive.

A common mistake is calling a repeating activity a project just because it has a budget, or calling a whole portfolio a single project. A team run as an operation with no end date never reaches closure, and applying an adaptive approach to a fixed-price contract often creates disputes over scope. Classify the work first, and the delivery approach and management language follow from that choice.

questions.prompt: A charity runs a food bank that hands out parcels every Tuesday with no planned end date. Separately, it is building a new volunteer-scheduling tool with a defined finish date and one finished tool as the result. Step 1: the parcel distribution repeats every week with no finish line, so it is operations. Step 2: the scheduling tool is temporary and aimed at a unique result, so it is a project. Step 3: the charity is not yet sure what volunteers need, and they will refine the tool after each trial release. Step 4: which delivery approach fits the scheduling tool, and why?
choices: Predictive, because a tool should always have its full plan fixed before any building starts
Operations, because volunteers will use the tool every week
Program, because the tool must be grouped with the parcel distribution
Adaptive, because unclear requirements refined through feedback suit short iterations
questions.why: Requirements that are unclear and will be refined as feedback arrives are the situation where adaptive delivery, using short iterations and regular plan adjustment, is the better fit.

questions.prompt: A regional museum runs daily ticket sales that have no end date. It also funds a four-month effort to replace its gift shop checkout system, with one finished system as the result. Which classification fits the checkout replacement?
choices: A portfolio, since the museum has chosen to fund it
A program, since it touches the same sales process as ticket sales
Operations, since daily sales repeat indefinitely and never reach a finish line
A project, since it has a finish point and a unique result
questions.why: A project is temporary work with an end point that produces a unique result, which describes the checkout replacement, whereas ongoing repeated sales are operations.

questions.prompt: A council hires a contractor for a fixed-price drainage repair, with specifications agreed in writing. Midway, the team starts changing scope through short iterations with no formal change control, and the council later disputes the final bill. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The council should have bought a portfolio of drainage contracts instead
The drainage repair was really an operation with no finish date
The contract was a program, so its scope could not be changed
Adaptive methods were used on a fixed-price contract
questions.why: Applying an adaptive approach to a fixed-price, predictive-style contract without formal control of scope changes is the failure pattern that produces disputes over scope.

questions.prompt: A software firm funds an office relocation, a rewrite of its customer app, and a payroll service it already runs each month. Which label best describes the full set of these items?
choices: A single project, because the firm funds them together
A program, because the payroll service and the app both rely on staff
A portfolio, because it is every chosen item ranked against strategy, whether or not the items are related
A program, because all three share one budget owner and one deadline
questions.why: A portfolio is the broadest view, covering all projects, programs and operations an organization has chosen to fund, and its items do not need to be related to each other.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says our quarterly payroll run is a project because it has a budget and a deadline every quarter. Explain to a teammate whether that is correct, and name one limit of the test you used to decide.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say payroll is operations, not a project. A project has a unique goal and a finish line once that goal is met, while payroll repeats the same routine every quarter with no end state. The budget and the deadline do not decide it, because operations also has budgets and fixed dates. The test I use is whether the work produces something new and closes, or keeps the business running. One limit of that test is that some work is mixed: replacing the payroll system is a project, while running payroll on the new system afterward is operations. So I would classify the specific work rather than the team label, and check whether it has a closure point before deciding how to manage it.
rubricPoints: Project work is temporary and produces a unique result with a defined end.
Operations is ongoing, repeating work with no finish line.
Budgets and deadlines alone do not make something a project.
Classify the specific work, since one area can contain both project and operations work.

suggested.rationale: Placing a situation correctly and justifying it aloud is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Projects run on four kinds of statements that sound alike but do different jobs. An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs fixing now. A risk is a possible future event that may never happen, but would hurt or help if it did. An assumption is something the team accepts as true for planning without having proven it. A constraint is a fixed limit the team must work inside, such as a deadline, a budget cap, or a rule. Reviewing a scope statement means checking it for what is vague, missing, or left unsaid.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your sponsor says the project must finish before the fiscal year ends in March. Is that a risk, a constraint, an assumption, or an issue? Give one reason for your choice.
lessons.teach:
An issue is a current problem: something has already happened or is happening and is affecting the project now. It needs an owner and an action. A risk is an uncertain future event. It has not happened, it may never happen, and if it does it can hurt the project (a threat) or help it (an opportunity). Risks are usually described with a likelihood and an impact. An assumption is a statement the team treats as true for planning without proof, such as 'the client's data team will be available in June.' Assumptions are not yet facts; if one turns out false, it becomes an issue or a new risk. A constraint is a limit the project must work within: a fixed deadline, a budget ceiling, a regulation, or a capped number of people. Constraints shape which options are allowed.

Why the split matters: issues get a fix and an owner, risks get a response plan and monitoring, assumptions get written down and validated so they do not hide, and constraints define the boundaries of every choice.

Worked example. A scope statement says: 'Deliver a reporting dashboard by June 30 using the vendor's team of four.' Step 1: 'June 30' is a constraint, a fixed limit. Step 2: 'the vendor's team of four' is an assumption, because nobody has confirmed the team will stay. Step 3: 'the vendor may be pulled to another client next quarter' is a risk, uncertain and in the future. Step 4: 'the vendor already lost a developer last week' is an issue, because it has happened.

Common mistake: calling every worry a risk. Something that has already happened is an issue, even if people still talk about it as a possibility.

Reviewing a scope statement for gaps means checking whether each deliverable has acceptance criteria, whether exclusions are stated, and whether the assumptions and constraints behind the plan are recorded. Gaps like these are where later disputes begin.

Consequence: if the lost developer is logged as a risk, nobody is assigned to act, and the schedule slips while the team waits to see what happens.

questions.prompt: A city council is replacing paper parking permits with a mobile app. The scope statement reads: 'Launch the permit app for all 12 districts by 1 November, built by the council's two in-house developers. The council has capped the project at $180,000. The council's IT lead assumes the existing payment gateway will handle peak traffic. Last Tuesday, one of the two developers was moved to another project and is no longer available. The payment provider has said it may raise its fees if a national regulation changes in January.' Worked through: Step 1, the 1 November launch date and the $180,000 cap are constraints, fixed limits that shape the options. Step 2, the assumption that the payment gateway handles peak traffic is untested, so it is an assumption. Step 3, the developer being moved away last Tuesday has already happened, so it is an issue. Step 4 is left for you: which item is the risk?
choices: The $180,000 spending cap, because it limits which options are allowed
The belief that the payment gateway will handle peak traffic, because nobody has verified it yet
The possible payment fee increase tied to a January regulation change, because it is uncertain and lies in the future
The developer who was moved to another project, because it needs an owner and an action now
questions.why: A risk is an uncertain future event, and a possible fee increase depending on a January regulation change fits that description, while the other three items are an issue, a constraint, and an assumption.

questions.prompt: A library renovation plan includes these four statements. Which one is an assumption rather than a constraint?
choices: Two volunteers already quit last month and were not replaced
Building permits must cost no more than $12,000 in total
The library must stay closed for no more than three weeks
The city's structural engineer will sign off the plans by March
questions.why: An assumption is something the team treats as true for planning without proof, and a sign-off expected by March is not yet confirmed, whereas the closure limit and the permit ceiling are fixed limits and the volunteers quitting has already happened.

questions.prompt: A team logs 'our lead designer resigned this week' in its risk register and waits to see whether it causes delays. What is the main problem with this entry?
choices: It is a constraint, because a resignation limits which people can be assigned
It is correctly logged, because staff departures are always risks until the replacement starts
It has already happened, so it is an issue that needs an owner and an action now
It is an assumption, because nobody has confirmed the designer's last day
questions.why: A risk is uncertain and has not happened, so a resignation that has already occurred is an issue, and logging it as a risk leaves no one assigned to act.

questions.prompt: A reviewer checks a scope statement for a regional bus company's new ticketing system. Which set of checks best describes a gap review of that statement?
choices: Confirm each deliverable has a per-developer salary figure, the team's preferred tools are named, and the vendor's logo appears
Confirm the risk likelihood scores are above 50 percent, the budget is rounded to the nearest thousand, and the sponsor has signed
Confirm the schedule has no more than five milestones, the stakeholders are listed alphabetically, and the meeting notes are filed
Confirm each deliverable has acceptance criteria, confirm exclusions are stated, and confirm the assumptions and constraints behind the plan are recorded
questions.why: Reviewing a scope statement for gaps means checking acceptance criteria, stated exclusions, and recorded assumptions and constraints, because missing items there are where later disputes begin.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how you would tell apart an issue, a risk, an assumption, and a constraint, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on assumptions in a plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would sort each statement by timing and certainty. If it has already happened and is hurting us now, it is an issue, so it needs an owner and a fix. If it is a possible future event, it is a risk, and I would note its likelihood, its impact, and a response. If the team is taking something as true without proof, it is an assumption, and I would write it down so it can be checked. If it is a fixed limit we must respect, like a deadline or a budget ceiling, it is a constraint. The tradeoff with assumptions is that they let us plan while information is incomplete, but they can quietly be wrong. A plan built on an unvalidated assumption looks solid until that assumption fails, and then the team discovers the gap as an issue rather than as a risk it could have prepared for.
rubricPoints: Issue: already happened and needs action now.
Risk: uncertain future event, described by likelihood and impact.
Assumption: taken as true for planning without proof, and must be validated.
Constraint: a fixed limit the project must work within.
Tradeoff: assumptions make planning possible but can hide errors until they become issues.

suggested.rationale: Sorting realistic mixed statements from a scenario adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this project management vocabulary.

lessons.plain: A project is a temporary effort to create something new or change how things work, and it has a defined end. Ethics here means the choices a project manager makes when no rule covers the exact situation: being honest about status, treating people fairly, respecting other people's views, and taking responsibility for outcomes. Professional conduct means holding to those expectations every day, not only when someone is checking. Projects also matter because they are the main vehicle organizations use to change: a new system, a new process, or a merged team. Seeing a project as a vehicle for change helps you ask what the organization is trying to become, not only whether the deliverable shipped.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project manager learns that a vendor delay will push the go-live date past a promise made to a key customer. The sponsor asks that the next status report stay optimistic until the vendor confirms a new date. What should the project manager do first, and why?
lessons.teach:
The PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct is a published set of values and standards that members and certification holders agree to follow. In plain terms, it describes four value areas: responsibility (owning your decisions and their results), respect (treating people and their input with regard), fairness (making decisions without favoritism or hidden bias, and handling conflicts of interest openly), and honesty (telling the truth and not misleading people, including by leaving things out). Some standards are mandatory, meaning you must do them. Others are aspirational, meaning they describe the conduct you should strive for.

Why it matters on a project: the project manager often holds information that others lack, and the people who depend on that information cannot check it for themselves. Ethics is how you decide what to disclose, to whom, and when.

Worked example. Step 1: the facts are that the vendor's dated plan shows a three-week slip and the customer promise is at risk. Step 2: honesty applies. An optimistic status report that hides a known slip misleads stakeholders, even if every sentence is technically true. Step 3: responsibility applies. The project manager owns accurate reporting, so the slip goes into the report with the real date. Step 4: respect and fairness apply. The sponsor has authority over how and when the customer is told, so the project manager escalates with options such as a reduced scope or added resources instead of making that call alone.

Common mistake: reading ethics as only avoiding outright lies. Omitting a known risk, or framing bad news so it looks better than it is, also breaches honesty.

Consequence in a running system: if the slip stays hidden, the operations team schedules its change freeze and staffing for the original date, and the new system goes live without warning. Support is unprepared, and the first outage lands on the customers the promise was meant to protect.

Ethical conduct protects the people who must act on a project's information, and an honest report is what lets them act in time.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm is rolling out warehouse-scanning software across 14 sites. The team lead learns that the vendor's signed delivery plan puts the final integration at 9 March, but the vendor's latest test log shows it cannot finish before 30 March, which is three weeks late. The site rollout date promised to the operations director is 12 March. Step 1: the facts are that the vendor's dated plan and test log disagree, and the promised date is at risk. Step 2: honesty applies. A status line that repeats the old 9 March date while knowing about the test log would mislead the operations director, even if every sentence in it is technically accurate. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: respect and fairness apply. The operations director has authority over how and when the site managers are told, so the team lead escalates with options such as a phased rollout or added vendor engineers rather than deciding alone. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Responsibility applies: the team lead should keep the 9 March date in the report and add the new date in an appendix that few people read.
Responsibility applies: the team lead should wait one more week to see whether the vendor recovers before changing the report.
Responsibility applies: the team lead owns accurate reporting, so the status report shows the 30 March date that the test log supports.
Responsibility applies: the team lead should send the new date only to the vendor's account manager, since the vendor owns the delivery plan.
questions.why: Responsibility means owning your decisions and their results, and for a project manager that includes putting the real, evidence-backed date into the report.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches the difference between mandatory and aspirational standards in the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct?
choices: Mandatory standards are the ones a project manager may set aside when a sponsor approves, while aspirational standards must always be followed.
Mandatory standards cover the four value areas, while aspirational standards cover only honesty and responsibility.
Mandatory standards are things you must do, while aspirational standards describe the conduct you should strive for.
Mandatory standards apply only to certification holders, while aspirational standards apply only to members who have not yet been certified.
questions.why: The teaching text defines mandatory standards as required and aspirational standards as conduct to strive for, and the other options invent conditions the text never states.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling-system project manager tells the steering group that testing is on track. Each sentence in the report is true, but the report leaves out that 40 critical defects remain open with no fix date. Which analysis best describes what went wrong?
choices: Respect was breached, because the report did not include the testing team's own wording about the defects.
Nothing was breached, because no sentence in the report was false and the steering group could ask questions.
Fairness was breached, because the project manager gave the steering group more information than the vendor.
Honesty was breached, because leaving out a known risk misleads stakeholders even when every sentence is true.
questions.why: The teaching text says honesty includes leaving things out, so omitting known open defects breaches honesty even though no sentence is false.

questions.prompt: A bank's project manager learns that a regulatory-reporting integration will slip by 10 working days. The sponsor has authority over how and when the regulator and the executive board are told. Which action best applies the code?
choices: Keep the original date in all reports until the fix is confirmed, so the executive board is not alarmed unnecessarily.
Report the real 10-day slip to the sponsor with the facts, and escalate options such as reduced scope or added testers instead of deciding the communication alone.
Contact the regulator directly with the new date, so the regulator hears the news before anyone can soften it.
Tell the executive board the slip is minor and let the sponsor find out later, to keep the project moving.
questions.why: The sponsor controls how and when stakeholders are told, so the project manager reports the true slip and escalates options rather than making that call alone or hiding the facts.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says ethics is just about not lying, so the professional code does not change how we handle a scope change. Explain to them, in your own words, how the code applies to a project decision, and name one limit or tradeoff of applying it strictly.
lessons.modelAnswer: The code is broader than not lying. It asks you to be honest in what you report and what you leave out, to take responsibility for the decisions you own, and to treat stakeholders fairly. For a scope change, that means showing the real effect on cost, schedule, and risk instead of quietly absorbing the extra work or framing the request to get it approved. It also means being open about any conflict of interest, such as a vendor you favor, and giving every stakeholder the same information. One tradeoff is speed. Full disclosure and broad consultation can slow a decision that the sponsor needs quickly, and a strict reading can make a project manager look obstructive. The practical answer is to disclose completely and escalate clearly, while letting the people with authority decide the timing and the response.
rubricPoints: Explains that ethics covers honesty in what is omitted or framed, not just outright lies
Connects the code to a specific project decision such as a scope change or status report
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as speed of decisions or pressure from stakeholders
Notes that the project manager discloses fully but the sponsor or authority holder decides the response

suggested.rationale: Applying the code and describing project change are best shown by explaining a scenario back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective.

lessons.plain: Every project needs a written plan that says how the work will be paid for, how good the result must be, how uncertainty will be handled, and how long the work will take. Think of a home renovation: the plan sets the budget, the finish standard, the list of things that could go wrong, and the timeline the builder will hold to. A separate plan describes what the finished house is for and how it will change after move-in. Mixing the two up leads people to manage the wrong thing. This lesson explains what the cost, quality, risk and schedule parts of the project plan are for, and how that plan differs from a product plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new mobile app with a fixed launch date and an approved budget. Which document should say how they will keep spending within that budget and decide what counts as good enough to ship: the product roadmap or the project management plan? Give your reason in one sentence.
lessons.teach:
A project management plan is the document, assembled during planning, that describes how a project will be executed, monitored, controlled and closed. It is built from subsidiary plans, one per area of management. Four of them matter here. The cost management plan sets how the budget is estimated, approved, tracked and controlled. The quality management plan defines what good means for the deliverables and how they will be checked. The risk management plan sets how uncertain events are identified, assessed and responded to. The schedule management plan sets how activities are sequenced, estimated and tracked against dates. The approved versions of scope, schedule and cost are called baselines, and they are the reference points against which actual performance is measured.

Why it works: a plan turns agreements into measurable comparisons. Without an approved cost baseline, an overrun cannot be detected. Without quality criteria, done means whatever the last person thought.

Worked example: the approved budget is 100,000 spread evenly over 10 weeks, so 40,000 is planned for week 4. Actual spend at the end of week 4 is 46,000. Step 1: the variance is 46,000 minus 40,000, which is 6,000 over. Step 2: that is 15 percent over the planned figure. Step 3: the cost plan says any variance above 10 percent is escalated to the sponsor, so the project manager escalates it.

Common mistake: treating a risk list as the risk management plan. The list is one output. The plan describes the method.

Consequence: a product roadmap describes what the product should do over its life, while the project plan describes how this piece of work will be delivered. If the schedule baseline is missing, the team cannot tell whether a slipped date threatens a launch window or a cutover.

questions.prompt: A library's website redesign has an approved budget of 60,000 spread evenly over 6 weeks, so 10,000 is planned per week. At the end of week 3, actual spend is 33,000. Step 1: planned spend at the end of week 3 is 30,000. Step 2: the variance is 3,000 over plan. Step 3 is missing: the cost plan says any variance above 5 percent of the planned figure is escalated to the sponsor. Which choice supplies the missing step and its result?
choices: Divide the variance by the planned 30,000 to get 10 percent, which is above the 5 percent rule, so the project manager escalates it to the sponsor.
Divide the variance by the total 60,000 budget to get 5 percent, which is not above the rule, so no escalation is needed.
Ignore the variance, because 3,000 is less than one week of planned spend of 10,000, so it is within tolerance.
Reset the cost baseline to 33,000 so that future spend is measured against actual figures.
questions.why: The rule measures variance as a percentage of the planned figure at that point, and 3,000 divided by 30,000 is 10 percent, which exceeds the 5 percent threshold and therefore goes to the sponsor.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a quality management plan?
choices: The rules that define what good means for deliverables and how they will be checked.
The sequence of activities and the dates on which each one is expected to finish.
A running count of defects found so far, which shows how the team is doing.
The approved budget figure and the date each payment is due to vendors.
questions.why: A quality management plan defines what good means for the deliverables and how they will be checked, while the other options describe outputs, budget items, or schedule content.

questions.prompt: A team reaches week 6 and reports the project is on track because no stakeholder has complained. Which gap in the project management plan explains why this claim cannot be checked?
choices: No schedule management plan, so the activities cannot be listed in any order.
No quality criteria, so done has no agreed meaning to compare against.
No cost management plan, so spending cannot be authorised by anyone.
No risk management plan, so no one has listed the uncertain events.
questions.why: Without quality criteria, done means whatever the last person thought, so there is no measurable reference for saying the work is on track.

questions.prompt: A hospital's software group has a three-year product roadmap and is running a four-month migration with a fixed cutover date. Which element of the project management plan would show whether the migration is threatening the cutover?
choices: The product roadmap itself, since it describes what the product should do over its life.
The schedule baseline, the approved reference dates for the migration activities.
The quality management plan, since it sets how deliverables will be checked.
A list of stakeholder complaints gathered in the last month.
questions.why: The schedule baseline holds the approved dates for this piece of work, so slipped dates can be measured against it, whereas the product roadmap describes the product's life rather than this delivery.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the project management plan and the product roadmap are the same document under different names, so the team only needs one. Explain to them, in your own words, how the two differ, what the cost, quality, risk and schedule parts of the project plan are for, and one limit or tradeoff of keeping them separate.
lessons.modelAnswer: They are different because they answer different questions. The project management plan covers how this piece of work will be delivered: the budget and its baseline, the quality criteria, the way risks are handled, and the schedule. It is about executing and controlling the project inside its constraints. The product roadmap covers what the product should do and why, over a longer period, including features and how value is delivered after launch. The cost, quality, risk and schedule parts exist so the team can compare actual results with approved baselines and act early. One tradeoff of keeping them separate is that the two can drift apart, so a feature on the roadmap may not fit the project's budget or date. The project manager has to check the two regularly and raise conflicts with the sponsor.
rubricPoints: The project management plan governs how a project is delivered and controlled, while the product roadmap describes what the product is for and how it evolves.
Cost, quality, risk and schedule subsidiary plans each define a method, and each supports comparison against approved baselines.
Baselines make variance visible, so problems can be escalated early.
Keeping the two plans separate creates a risk that they drift apart and need reconciling.

suggested.rationale: Telling the two plans apart and justifying the purpose of each area is an explanation skill, and explaining it back to a teammate tests it directly.

lessons.plain: A project plan has two kinds of time-related items that are easy to confuse. A milestone is a point in time that marks something reached or finished, such as a signed-off design, and it has no length of its own. A task duration is how long a piece of work takes, measured in days or hours. Sizing resources means counting how many people, with which skills, the work needs and when. A risk register is a running list of things that could go wrong, and a stakeholder register is a list of the people and groups who affect the project or are affected by it. Together these show what must happen, how long it takes, who is needed, and what could derail it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your schedule lists 'Design approved' with a duration of 0 days, and 'Write the API' with a duration of 10 days. Which line is the milestone, and why might the zero-day line matter more to your sponsor than the 10-day line?
lessons.teach:
A milestone is a significant point in the project schedule, such as an approval, a delivery, or a go-live decision. It marks that something has been reached, and it has zero duration because it describes a moment rather than work. A task is an activity that produces part of the outcome and takes time, measured as its duration, which is the elapsed working time from start to finish. Effort is different again: it is the labour hours put in, and it can differ from duration when several people work in parallel or someone works part-time.

Resource sizing means estimating how many people, with which skills, and for how long the project needs them. It works because the number of people available at any moment limits which tasks can run at once, so a schedule that ignores who is free is not realistic. A resource calendar records when each person is available.

A risk register is a log of identified uncertainties, each with a description, a likelihood, an impact, an owner, and a planned response. A stakeholder register lists the people and groups who can affect the project or be affected by it, with their interest, their influence, and what they need to know.

Worked example: a three-person team plans a website launch. Task A, 'Write content', takes 6 working days for one writer. Task B, 'Build pages', takes 8 days for one developer. Milestone 'Content approved' follows Task A and has zero duration. Step by step: the approver, a designer, is on leave for 4 days. The team records this in the risk register with an owner and a response, which is to book the approval before the leave starts. The milestone date moves only if the approval slips, so the register keeps that dependency visible.

Common mistake: writing 'Approval: 3 days' as a task. This hides the real wait on someone outside the team and makes the milestone look like work the team controls. Another frequent mistake is filling in a risk register once and never reviewing it.

Consequence: a project whose risk register goes unreviewed keeps promising dates that a known blocker already threatens, so the sponsor hears about the slip late.

Keeping milestones as zero-length points, sizing people against a real calendar, and reviewing both registers together is what makes a schedule trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team is planning a new stock-tracking system. Task C, 'Clean item records', takes 10 working days, and two analysts work on it at the same time, each full-time. Step 1: the duration of Task C is 10 working days, the elapsed time from start to finish. Step 2: the effort is the labour put in, which is 2 analysts working 10 days each, so 20 person-days. Step 3: Milestone 'Barcode format confirmed' follows a supplier's written confirmation, which is expected but not yet received. Missing step: what duration should the milestone 'Barcode format confirmed' carry on the schedule?
choices: 20 person-days, copied from the effort of Task C
10 working days, matching the duration of the task before it
2 working days, to allow for the supplier's usual reply time
Zero, because a milestone marks a point reached rather than work done over time
questions.why: A milestone is a moment that marks something reached, so it has zero duration, and any waiting time belongs in the risk register or as a separate tracked item rather than inside the milestone.

questions.prompt: A task is planned to take 5 working days. Two people work on it full-time at the same time for the whole period. Which pair of figures is correct?
choices: Duration 10 days, effort 5 person-days
Duration 5 days, effort 5 person-days
Duration 5 days, effort 10 person-days
Duration 2.5 days, effort 5 person-days
questions.why: Duration is the elapsed time from start to finish, which stays 5 days, while effort is the total labour hours, which is 2 people times 5 days, or 10 person-days.

questions.prompt: A school district is changing its bell timetable. A parent council is strongly interested in the change and affected by it, but has little say over the budget or the final decision. Which stakeholder register entry best describes the council?
choices: Interest low, influence high, needs no updates
Interest high, influence low, needs regular updates on timing and changes
Interest high, influence high, needs a formal sign-off role
Interest low, influence low, not worth listing in the register
questions.why: A stakeholder register records each group's interest, influence, and information needs, and a group that is strongly affected but has little power should be listed with high interest, low influence, and a need for updates.

questions.prompt: A software project lists this risk: 'The lead engineer may resign before testing ends.' Which version gives the complete risk register entry the teaching text describes?
choices: Description, likelihood, impact, owner, and planned response, such as the project manager tracking retention plans with HR
Description, impact, and owner, with the response left for the team to decide later
Description and likelihood only, to be reviewed when the schedule is baselined
Description only: the lead engineer may resign before testing ends
questions.why: A risk register entry needs a description, likelihood, impact, owner, and planned response together, and only the option that includes all five gives that complete record.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a milestone differs from a task duration, and how the risk register and stakeholder register should change the way you size resources. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on these registers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A milestone is a point that marks something reached, like an approval, so it has zero duration and no work of its own. A task duration is how long a piece of work takes. When I size resources, I look at who is actually available on the calendar, because a schedule that assumes everyone is free is not realistic. The risk register tells me which availability gaps could move dates, such as a key approver on leave, and gives each one an owner and a response. The stakeholder register tells me who has to approve or be informed, so I can plan their time too. The main limit is that both registers are only as good as their upkeep: they are snapshots that go stale quickly, and a stakeholder who is missing from the list will not get the planning they need. So I review them at a regular checkpoint, not just at the start.
rubricPoints: A milestone is a zero-duration point marking a reached state, while a task duration is elapsed time for work
Resource sizing must account for each person's availability and skills, not just headcount
The risk register records uncertainties with owners and responses that can change dates
The stakeholder register identifies who affects or is affected by the project and shapes planning
A stated limit: registers go stale unless they are reviewed on a regular schedule

suggested.rationale: Explaining milestones, durations, resource sizing, and registers back to a teammate with a tradeoff is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers project planning.

lessons.plain: Closing a project means finishing it on purpose rather than letting it fade out. Once the work is built and accepted, the team confirms the customer agrees the result is done, hands the result to the people who will run and use it, pays final bills and closes contracts, releases staff and equipment, and records what went well and what did not so future projects benefit. Transition is the part where ownership moves from the project team to the ongoing operations group. Think of moving into a new house: you do not just leave the keys on the table. You sign the paperwork, explain how the heating works, and tell the new owners where the spare parts are.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has finished building and testing a new customer web form, and the developers say they are done and want to start their next project. What is one thing that still needs to happen before this project can truly be called closed, and why?
lessons.teach:
Project closure is the set of formal activities that end a project after its work is complete. A project has a defined end, so it needs a deliberate finish. Without one, costs keep running, nobody clearly owns the result, and lessons are lost. Final acceptance is the customer or sponsor formally approving the deliverables against the agreed criteria. Transition, sometimes called handover, is moving ownership of the result to the group that will operate and support it, along with documentation, training, and access. Administrative closure covers archiving records, writing the final report, and releasing team members and equipment. Contract closure settles vendor agreements and final invoices. Lessons learned is a structured review of what worked and what did not, stored for future projects.

Worked example: a team builds a payroll report tool. First, they check each acceptance criterion and the finance manager signs acceptance. Second, they hand the operations group a runbook, hold a recorded training session, and confirm that group can run the tool alone. Third, they pay the final vendor invoice and close the license contract. Fourth, they release the team to other work and hold a lessons learned session, which records that requirements changed late, so next time scope will be locked earlier. Fifth, they archive the project records.

Common mistake: treating a passing build as closure. The result is that nobody owns the tool after launch, and support requests go unanswered.

Consequence in a running system: if transition is skipped, the on-call team is paged for a service they never learned to operate, and vendor charges continue to accrue. Closure is complete only when acceptance, handover, and the financial and administrative close are all done.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union builds a scanner that files loan paperwork into its document system. The team works through closure in four steps. Step 1: the branch operations manager checks each agreed criterion and signs formal acceptance. Step 2: the team gives the IT service desk a support guide and confirms the desk can restart the scanning service without the project team. Step 3 is missing. It is the step that closes the scanning-software vendor's agreement and settles its last invoice. Step 4: the team releases two contractors and the shared test server, then archives the project folder. Which action best describes the missing step 3 in this closure sequence?
choices: Ask the vendor to extend its support term by another six months before paying.
Confirm the vendor's final invoice is paid and its agreement is formally ended.
Remove the scanning software from the test server so it is not reused.
Run a short lessons learned session and store the notes in the project archive.
questions.why: The missing step is contract closure, which settles the vendor agreement and final invoice, and that is the only option that describes this.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines transition, also called handover, in project closure?
choices: Sending the final project report to the sponsor for filing.
Paying the last vendor invoice and ending the software licence.
Moving ownership of the result to the group that will run and support it, with documentation, training, and access.
Recording what went well and badly so future projects can use it.
questions.why: Transition is defined as moving ownership of the result, plus its documentation, training, and access, to the operating group.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain's booking chatbot passed every test, and the project team was reassigned the same day. The chatbot is live, but the hotel's service desk has never been trained on it, and the vendor's monthly fee is still being billed. Which closure work is still incomplete?
choices: Only the final acceptance by the sponsor.
Only the administrative archive of the project records.
Handover to the operating group and the contract and financial close, in addition to acceptance.
Only the lessons learned review.
questions.why: A passing build is not closure: handover and the financial and contract close remain open, so the operating group and the vendor billing are not yet settled.

questions.prompt: A school district's timetable app project finished late after requirements kept changing, and the team skipped the lessons learned session to save time. What is the most likely consequence for the district's next timetable project?
choices: The next project may repeat the late scope changes, because the cause was never recorded or stored for future use.
The sponsor will be unable to give final acceptance to the next project.
The next team will be unable to release its staff to other work.
The vendor will refuse to send a final invoice for the license.
questions.why: Lessons learned is stored for future projects, so skipping it means the cause of late changes is not captured and the next team may repeat it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says closing the project just means turning off time tracking and sending a thank-you email. In your own words, explain to them what project closure and transition involve, and name one limit or tradeoff a closing project faces, such as how much time to spend on lessons learned or what to do with unfinished scope.
lessons.modelAnswer: Closure is more than admin. Before the project ends, the sponsor or customer has to formally accept the deliverables against the agreed criteria. Then transition moves ownership to the operations team, which needs documentation, training, and access so it can run the result without help from the project team. After that, we settle contracts and final invoices, release the people and equipment, archive the records, and hold a lessons learned review. The tradeoff is time: lessons learned and documentation take effort when the team is already eager to move on, so the review should stay short and focused on a few decisions that would change next time. Unfinished scope is another limit. It should be formally moved to a future project or to operations with a named owner, not quietly dropped at closure.
rubricPoints: Names formal acceptance of deliverables by the customer or sponsor as a closure step
Explains transition or handover, including documentation, training, and ownership moving to operations
Mentions administrative and contract closure, such as releasing resources and settling vendor invoices
Gives a realistic limit or tradeoff, such as time for lessons learned or handling unfinished scope

suggested.rationale: Explaining closure and handover back to a teammate, including tradeoffs, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: A project has several people with different jobs. The project manager plans the work, keeps it moving, and answers for getting it done within agreed limits. The project sponsor is usually a senior person who funds the project, cares about the business result, and settles big decisions or approves major changes. The project team is everyone who does the hands-on work, such as analysts, designers, developers, and testers. A project manager does not act one way all the time. Depending on the moment, they may start the project, negotiate with people who want different things, listen closely to concerns, coach a teammate, run a meeting, or pitch in on the work themselves. Knowing who decides what keeps people from waiting on the wrong person.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer on a project believes the agreed budget is too small to finish the work. Who should they raise this with first: the project manager, the project sponsor, or another team member? Give your reasoning in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A project sponsor is the senior person or group who champions the project, provides funding, and cares most about the business result it should produce. The project manager, usually shortened to PM, is the person assigned to lead the work. They plan it, track it, manage risks and communication, and are accountable for delivering it within agreed scope, time, and cost. The project team is the group doing the work, such as analysts, designers, developers, and testers, who carry out tasks and report progress.

The split works because each role owns a different kind of decision. The sponsor decides whether the project is still worth continuing and whether major changes to money or purpose are acceptable. The PM decides how the work is organised day to day, inside those limits. The team decides how individual tasks are built.

The PM also plays several roles in one day. As initiator, they help start the project and get it formally authorised. As negotiator, they trade scope, dates, and resources with stakeholders. As listener, they hear concerns early. As coach, they help team members grow. As facilitator, they run meetings so decisions actually get made. As working team member, they sometimes do hands-on work themselves.

Worked example: A reporting project is three weeks late because a data vendor slipped. The PM, Ana, listens to the lead engineer's explanation, negotiates a smaller first release with the business owner, and facilitates a short meeting to agree a new plan. She does not approve extra budget herself. She takes that request to the sponsor, who approves it or declines it.

Common mistake: treating the PM as the boss who decides everything, or treating the sponsor as the person who should run the daily stand-up. Each mix-up delays decisions and blurs accountability.

In a running system, a funding or scope change that sits with the wrong person can leave a release stuck for weeks while the team waits for an answer that nobody with authority has given.

The PM owns the plan, the sponsor owns the funding and the business outcome, and the team owns the work.

questions.prompt: At a tutoring-app company, Priya is the project manager for a shift-scheduling feature. Step one: she finds that the new feature needs a different login method, which adds about £12,000 to the budget. Step two: she takes that request to the sponsor, Dr. Osei, who approves it. Step three: she sets up a weekly coaching slot for a junior developer who is unsure how authentication works. The missing step is how the authentication code itself is structured, meaning the design of the individual tasks. Which completion correctly fills that gap?
choices: The developer doing the work decides the code structure, with review from the lead, because the team decides how individual tasks are built.
Dr. Osei decides the code structure, because the sponsor owns the business outcome and therefore the design.
Priya decides the code structure herself, because the PM owns every technical decision on the project.
The junior developer's coach decides the code structure, because coaching includes choosing the implementation.
questions.why: The team owns how individual tasks are built, while the PM owns the day-to-day plan and the sponsor owns funding and the business result.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly pairs a role with the decision it owns?
choices: The PM decides whether the project should be funded at all.
The sponsor decides how each task is coded.
The team decides whether the business case still holds.
The sponsor decides whether the project is still worth continuing and whether major changes to money or purpose are acceptable.
questions.why: The sponsor owns continuation and major funding or purpose changes, while the PM owns day-to-day organisation and the team owns task construction.

questions.prompt: On a tutoring-app project, a PM notices a developer freezing when asked to write automated tests. She sets up two pairing sessions a week to work through test design with him. Which PM role is she mainly playing?
choices: Initiator, because she is helping start the project formally.
Coach, because she is helping a team member grow.
Negotiator, because she is trading scope or dates with stakeholders.
Facilitator, because she is running a meeting so a decision gets made.
questions.why: Setting up regular sessions to build a team member's skill is the coach role, distinct from running meetings or trading scope.

questions.prompt: On a bus dispatch project, a team lead asks for a 40 percent budget increase. The PM, Sam, approves it on the spot to avoid delay. What is the main problem?
choices: Sam should have refused without consulting anyone, because budgets are fixed once set.
There is no problem, because the PM owns the plan and so the budget is hers to give.
A funding change is the sponsor's decision, so the PM should take the request to the sponsor rather than approve it herself.
The team lead should have approved it, because the team owns the budget.
questions.why: Major changes to money belong to the sponsor, and a PM who approves them alone blurs accountability and can bypass the person with authority.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to projects how the project manager, the project sponsor, and the project team differ in responsibility, and name one limit on the project manager's authority.
lessons.modelAnswer: The sponsor is the senior stakeholder who funds the project and owns the business result, so they approve major changes to money or purpose. The project manager leads the work day to day: planning, tracking progress, managing risks and communication, and handling trade-offs within the limits the sponsor has set. The team does the hands-on work and makes the technical choices for its own tasks. The PM's main limit is authority. They can negotiate and reorganise the work, but they usually cannot approve extra budget or change the business goal alone. When a request needs more money, the PM takes it to the sponsor with options and a recommendation, rather than promising it or waiting silently.
rubricPoints: The sponsor funds the project and owns the business result, and approves major changes to money or purpose.
The project manager leads day-to-day planning, tracking, risk, and communication within agreed limits.
The project team carries out the hands-on tasks and makes technical choices for its own work.
The PM cannot usually approve extra budget or change the business goal alone and must escalate to the sponsor.

suggested.rationale: Explaining who decides what, and where a PM's authority stops, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it.

lessons.plain: Managing a project means keeping the work organized: making plans, tracking progress, and making sure things are done on time and within budget. Leading means giving people a direction worth following and getting them to commit to it, even when nobody is ordering them to. A project manager usually needs both. Emotional intelligence, often shortened to EQ, is the skill of noticing your own feelings and other people's, and responding to them sensibly. It shapes how bad news travels, how conflict gets handled, and whether people trust you enough to tell you the truth early. Two projects with identical plans can end very differently because of it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two project managers face the same late project. One updates the schedule and sends a reminder to the team; the other first asks the team what is making them hesitant to report problems. Which is more likely to surface the real cause of the delay, and why?
lessons.teach:
Management is the work of keeping projects predictable: planning tasks, organizing people and resources, and controlling progress against a baseline such as a schedule or budget. Leadership is the work of getting people to move in a shared direction: setting a vision, building trust, and influencing others without relying only on formal authority. Management asks whether the work is on track; leadership asks whether people are committed to getting it there.

Emotional intelligence (EQ) is the ability to recognize emotions in yourself and others, understand what they signal, and choose a response that serves the goal. It includes self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, and social skill in adjusting how you communicate.

Why it matters: project information moves from the people doing the work to the people deciding. People share bad news only when they expect a calm, fair response. A project manager with high EQ surfaces problems early; one without it finds them at the end.

Worked example. A developer reports on track each week, yet the test count has not changed in two weeks. Step 1: the manager notices the gap between the words and the data. Step 2: she asks him privately what is blocking progress, rather than challenging him in front of the team. Step 3: he admits the requirements were unclear and he feared saying so. Step 4: she clarifies them with the sponsor and re-baselines the schedule with an honest date.

Common mistake: treating EQ as being agreeable or avoiding conflict. Empathy does not mean dropping the goal; it means finding the real cause before pressing for the outcome.

Consequence: a team that hides problems is like a monitoring system with silenced alerts. The status board stays green until the failure arrives all at once.

Good project managers use management discipline to track the work and leadership with emotional intelligence to decide how and when to act on what the data shows.

questions.prompt: Yusuf manages a website redesign for a bakery chain. His six contractors have a sign-off milestone on Friday. The designer says sign-off is nearly done every week, yet the approval tracker has shown no approvals since the 3rd. Step 1: Yusuf compares the designer's words against the tracker and sees the gap. Step 2: He arranges a short one-on-one call and asks an open question about what is making sign-off hard, without raising the delay in front of the others. Step 3: The designer admits the brand colors were never confirmed and he did not want to look slow. Step 4 is missing: what should Yusuf do next to address the real cause and reset the plan?
choices: Get the brand owner to confirm the colors, then update the schedule with a realistic sign-off date.
Report the green status to the steering group so the contractors stay motivated.
Ask the designer to work weekends so the original Friday date holds without changing anything else.
Remove the designer from the team, since he hid the delay from the group.
questions.why: The missing step resolves the confirmed cause (unclear colors) and then re-baselines the schedule with an honest date, which is the same pattern of finding the cause before pressing for the outcome.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT rollout lead says her job is to keep the install on schedule and within budget, and also to win over nurses so they actually use the new system. Which statement best separates the two parts of her role?
choices: Both parts are the same task, because a project on schedule will automatically earn nurse adoption.
Tracking progress against the baseline is management, while setting a shared direction and building trust is leadership.
Leadership means reporting status accurately, and management means persuading people to change how they work.
Keeping work on schedule and budget is leadership, and winning nurse commitment is management.
questions.why: Management is planning, organizing, and controlling progress against a baseline, while leadership is setting a vision and building trust so people commit to the direction.

questions.prompt: A team lead at a regional insurance firm avoids raising any disagreement with his analysts, so meetings stay pleasant and no one argues. Work slips for weeks before anyone mentions it. Which description best matches the emotional intelligence failure here?
choices: He is practicing empathy, because he does not want to upset anyone on the team.
He is correctly using social skill to adjust how he communicates bad news.
He is treating EQ as agreeableness, which drops the goal instead of finding the real cause of the slip.
He is showing high self-regulation by keeping the mood steady.
questions.why: Confusing EQ with being agreeable or avoiding conflict is the common mistake; genuine empathy finds the real cause of a problem and still pursues the outcome.

questions.prompt: A mobile app team at a grocery delivery startup reports green status every Monday. The project lead notices that the bug count has risen for three weeks, and one developer seems withdrawn in standups. Which first action best uses emotional intelligence while still keeping the work on track?
choices: Announce the rising bug count in the team channel so everyone sees the problem at once.
Ignore the mood signals and keep the green status until the data forces a change.
Privately ask the withdrawn developer what is blocking progress, then compare the answer with the bug trend.
Move the developer to a different team, since the withdrawn behavior is likely a personal issue.
questions.why: Recognizing the emotional signal and asking privately to find the real cause is the high-EQ response that surfaces problems early without dropping the goal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks project managers only need planning skills: how is leadership different from management, how does emotional intelligence affect project outcomes, and what limit or tradeoff should a project manager watch for when using EQ?
lessons.modelAnswer: Management keeps a project predictable: it plans the work, assigns resources, and checks progress against the schedule and budget. Leadership gives people a direction and a reason to commit, through trust and influence rather than authority alone. A project manager needs both, because a perfectly tracked plan still fails if the team hides problems or stops caring. Emotional intelligence affects outcomes because information only flows upward when people feel safe reporting bad news. A project manager who recognizes frustration or fear can ask the right private question and find a blocked requirement early. The tradeoff is that EQ can slide into avoiding hard decisions. Empathy should shape how and when a project manager acts, not whether the deadline or a scope decision gets addressed. Reading people is also a judgment call, so it should be checked against data rather than assumed.
rubricPoints: Management focuses on planning, organizing and controlling work against a baseline; leadership focuses on direction, trust and commitment.
A project manager needs both, since a well-tracked plan still fails if people hide problems.
EQ affects outcomes by shaping whether people share bad news early.
EQ should guide how and when to act, not replace decisions or scope discipline.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the leadership-management contrast and EQ's effect on outcomes back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: A project plan is a written set of decisions about how work will be done: who gets told what, how often, and how risks get spotted and handled. Following a planned strategy means doing what the plan says and checking whether it still fits reality, instead of inventing a new approach each week. Project initiation is the early step where a project is formally started, its purpose agreed, and a sponsor approves it. Planning turns that approval into a roadmap the team can follow. The benefit is that people know what to expect, decisions are made once rather than repeatedly, and problems are seen before they become emergencies.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of six starts a three-month project with no written plan for how they will share status or handle risks. Two months in, a supplier delivery slips and three people report three different new dates. What is the most likely underlying problem, and what would have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
A project management plan is the set of documents that says how a project will be run. Within it, a communication plan records who needs which information, in what format, and how often. A risk management plan records how risks will be identified, rated, and answered. Initiation is the step where a project is formally authorized, usually through a charter signed by a sponsor (the person who owns the business case and funds the work). Planning comes next and produces a baseline: the agreed scope, schedule, and cost that progress is measured against.

Why it works: a plan removes repeated decisions. When everyone knows the reporting rhythm and the escalation path, nobody has to invent one under pressure, and changes can be measured against the baseline instead of memory.

Worked example: a team of eight is replacing a vendor. Step 1: the charter names the sponsor and who can approve changes. Step 2: the communication plan says the vendor lead sends a status report every Tuesday by noon, and any risk above an agreed score goes to the sponsor within two working days. Step 3: in week five the vendor reports a delay. The project manager follows the plan: logs the risk in the risk register, notifies the sponsor within two days, and shows the schedule impact against the baseline. The sponsor chooses a fallback within the same week.

Common mistake: treating the plan as a document filed once and forgotten. Following a plan means checking it against reality and changing it through the agreed change process, not quietly ignoring it or rewriting it to match what happened.

Consequence: without a written communication plan, the delay in the example reaches the sponsor from three sources with three dates, and the fallback decision comes late.

Planned work is only as useful as the habit of following it and updating it on purpose.

questions.prompt: A regional library network is rolling out a new catalogue system with a team of five. The charter, signed by the network director who funds the work, names the director as the approver for scope changes. The communication plan says the software vendor's lead sends a written status update every Monday before 10:00. In week three, the Monday update reports that data migration will finish 6 working days later than the baseline finish date of 14 April. The project manager works through the response: first, the delay is recorded in the risk register and the vendor's report is filed with the date it arrived. Second, the new finish date is compared with the baseline to show the schedule impact, which is 6 working days. Third, [missing step]. Fourth, once the director approves, the revised date is recorded as the new baseline and the team continues.
choices: The project manager rewrites the baseline to 20 April immediately, so that future progress is measured against the new date and no further variance is reported.
The project manager holds the information until the next Monday update, to see whether the vendor recovers the lost days on its own.
The project manager asks the vendor to make up the 6 days by working weekends, without informing the director, to avoid a formal change.
The project manager sends a change request to the director named in the charter and waits for approval before altering the baseline.
questions.why: The charter names the director as approver, and the plan says the baseline changes only through the agreed change process, so the change request must go to that approver before the baseline is updated.

questions.prompt: In project management, what does a communication plan record?
choices: Who needs which information, in what format, and how often they receive it.
The signed agreement between the project and its external suppliers.
The cost of each team member's software licence and when it renews.
The list of risks ranked by their likelihood and impact on the budget.
questions.why: The text defines the communication plan as recording who needs which information, in what format, and how often, which matches the second option and no other.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling-software project has a risk plan that says any risk scored above 8 must go to the sponsor within two working days. The team logs a risk scored 11 on Wednesday morning. What should the project manager do first, according to the plan's logic?
choices: Fix the risk personally without telling the sponsor, since the team can handle it.
Escalate the risk to the sponsor, because the score is above the agreed threshold and the plan requires notice within two working days.
Wait until Friday to see whether the risk score changes before telling anyone.
Add the risk to the charter so that it becomes part of the project's approval.
questions.why: The risk management plan sets the threshold and the escalation timing, and a score of 11 is above the threshold of 8, so the plan calls for escalation to the sponsor within the set window.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm writes a communication plan and a risk plan at the start of a warehouse-automation project. Six weeks later, the scope has changed twice, but the plans have not been updated and the team still follows them as written. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The baseline stays fixed, so the team has no measurable way to show that the scope has changed.
The project moves into the portfolio level, where plans are no longer needed.
The sponsor's signature on the charter is automatically withdrawn.
The plans become more accurate because the team is following them without changes.
questions.why: Plans must be checked against reality and changed through the agreed process; if they are left stale, the baseline no longer reflects the agreed scope, so changes cannot be measured against it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague asks why we bother with initiation and planning when the team could just start working. Explain what a planned communication or risk approach does for the project, and name one limit or tradeoff of planning up front.
lessons.modelAnswer: Initiation gives the project a formal start: a purpose, a sponsor, and agreed authority. Planning then turns that into a baseline and a set of rules, such as who gets status reports, when, and how a risk gets escalated. The main benefit is that decisions are made once and reused, so when a supplier delays work, the project manager already knows who to tell and by when, and the sponsor hears about it early enough to choose a fallback. The tradeoff is that planning takes time before any visible progress, and a plan written too early can be out of date by the time work starts. So I would say we plan enough to make decisions in advance, then review the plan at set points and change it through the agreed process instead of ignoring it.
rubricPoints: Initiation formally authorizes the project and names a sponsor or authority.
Following a communication or risk plan means decisions and escalation paths are set in advance.
The baseline gives a fixed reference for measuring change and progress.
Planning has a cost: time before visible work, and plans can go stale.
Plans should be reviewed and changed through an agreed process, not ignored or quietly rewritten.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the benefit of planning to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A meeting is only worth its time if it produces something the group needed. This lesson is about judging whether a meeting worked and choosing the right format for a problem. Three common formats do different jobs. A focus group gathers opinions from a small chosen set of people about a product, process, or idea. A stand-up is a short daily check-in where each person says what they finished, what they will do next, and what is blocking them. A brainstorming session generates many ideas quickly without judging them yet. Picking the wrong format wastes people's time, even when everyone is polite.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team has held three long status meetings this week where nobody made a decision and the same issues came up again. Without any teaching, what would you check first to decide whether those meetings were effective, and what would you change?
lessons.teach:
Effectiveness of a meeting is judged by its purpose, not by how long it ran or how many people attended. Start by asking what the meeting was for: a decision, a set of ideas, a coordination check, or feedback on something. A meeting is effective when it leaves behind a visible result that the purpose called for, such as a decision recorded with an owner, a ranked list of ideas, or a blocker assigned to someone to remove.

A focus group is a small guided discussion with a selected set of people, usually to learn how they perceive a product, process, or proposed change. Its purpose is gathering perceptions. A facilitator, the person who guides the discussion, asks open questions and records answers. A focus group does not decide anything by itself. A stand-up, a short meeting common on agile teams and often held daily, has each member give three things: what they finished, what they plan next, and what is blocking them. Its purpose is coordination and surfacing problems early. A brainstorming session is built to generate many possible ideas quickly, and its rule is to postpone judgment: ideas are captured first and evaluated in a separate step.

Worked example: a team of six must reduce late deliveries. Step one, the facilitator states the purpose: produce candidate causes and fixes, not a final choice. Step two, the group brainstorms for fifteen minutes, writing every idea without criticism, and collects twenty-three items. Step three, duplicates are merged and the group votes on the top five. Step four, each chosen action gets an owner and a follow-up date. The meeting is effective because its output matches its purpose.

Common mistake: running a brainstorm as a debate, so people reject ideas as they appear and the list stays short. A related mistake is turning a stand-up into a status report for the manager, which makes a coordination check into a meeting of its own.

Consequence in a running project: a stand-up that hides a blocker lets a stalled task sit unnoticed until the delivery date is already at risk.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy team of four wants to cut dosing-label errors. The facilitator opens by stating the purpose: produce candidate fixes and pick one to pilot this month. Step two: the group brainstorms for ten minutes, writing every idea without comment, and collects twelve items. Step three is missing from this record. What should happen next so the meeting's output matches its stated purpose?
choices: Each pharmacist argues for their favourite idea until the group agrees, rejecting the rest as they come up.
The group holds a focus group with patients to learn how they perceive the labels, and stops there.
Duplicates are merged and the group chooses a short list of top ideas, then the chosen fix gets an owner and a follow-up date.
The group immediately sends all twelve ideas to the pharmacy director as final decisions without any ranking.
questions.why: Brainstorming postpones judgment, so evaluation and narrowing happen in a separate step after ideas are captured, and the chosen action needs an owner and follow-up to produce the result the purpose called for.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the main purpose of a focus group?
choices: To gather how selected people perceive a product, process, or proposed change.
To generate as many ideas as possible while withholding any judgment on them.
To make a final decision that the sponsor can sign off on the same day.
To coordinate what each team member finished, plans next, and is blocked on.
questions.why: A focus group is a small guided discussion whose purpose is gathering perceptions; it does not decide anything by itself.

questions.prompt: A team holds a daily stand-up. Each member reports to the department manager in turn, and the manager asks follow-up questions about each person's progress. A developer mentions being stuck on a missing test server, but nobody is assigned to fix it and the meeting moves on. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The stand-up is working as intended because the manager heard every update.
The meeting ran too long, so the team should cut the stand-up to two minutes.
The team needs a focus group to learn how developers perceive the test environment.
The stand-up has turned into a status report for the manager, and the blocker was surfaced but not turned into an assigned action.
questions.why: A stand-up's purpose is coordination and surfacing blockers, and a blocker that is raised without an owner to remove it is a missed result, while the manager-facing report is the common mistake the text describes.

questions.prompt: During a brainstorm on reducing warehouse picking errors, the team lead responds to each idea with a reason it will not work, so people stop offering ideas and the list ends at five items. Which change best fits the purpose of a brainstorm?
choices: Shorten the session to five minutes so that fewer objections come up in the room.
Limit each person to one idea so the lead can evaluate each one thoroughly as it is spoken.
Hold the critique in a separate step after the ideas are all captured, and let no one reject an idea during generation.
Keep the critique, but ask people to write their ideas on sticky notes so the lead reads them later.
questions.why: Brainstorming works by postponing judgment: ideas are captured first without criticism and then evaluated separately, which is what the lead's immediate rejections were undermining.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a meeting how you would tell whether a meeting was effective, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a focus group to inform a decision rather than a larger survey, or of using brainstorming to make a decision.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would judge a meeting by the result it was meant to produce, not by its length. First I would ask what the purpose was: decide, generate ideas, coordinate, or gather opinions. Then I would check whether that output exists, with an owner and a date attached.
