For a brainstorm, the test is whether we got many ideas without early rejection, and whether they were evaluated afterward in a separate step. For a focus group, the test is whether we learned how the people in the room perceive the issue. One limit of a focus group is that a small, hand-picked set of people may not represent the wider user base, and one or two strong voices can shape the answers. Its findings are a direction to test, not proof of what everyone thinks. A brainstorm is also a poor tool for making a single decision, because it deliberately produces options without ranking them.
rubricPoints: Judge a meeting's effectiveness by whether it produced the output its purpose required, such as a decision with an owner.
A focus group gathers perceptions from a small selected group and cannot by itself show what a wider population thinks.
A stand-up is a short coordination check covering finished work, next work, and blockers.
Brainstorming generates many ideas with judgment postponed, then evaluates them in a separate step.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission makes the learner run or judge a meeting, and the core skill here is explaining purpose and limits back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Some projects are planned almost completely at the start and then carried out in a set order, much like building a bridge from blueprints. Others are planned in short rounds and adjusted as the team learns. Choosing between these approaches depends partly on how the team is organized: whether people sit together or are spread across locations, whether they report to one boss or split loyalty between a department head and a project manager, and whether decisions flow down a single chain of command. This lesson is about recognizing when a plan-first approach fits that organizational setup, and when it does not.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of twelve people works in three countries, each member reports to a different department head, and the client wants a fixed scope and a fixed delivery date. Before reading on, which approach would you lean toward, and what single feature of that setup makes you lean that way?
lessons.teach:
A predictive, plan-based approach defines most of the scope, schedule and cost early, then carries out the work in a largely fixed sequence, with changes handled through a formal review. An adaptive approach works in short cycles and refines the plan as feedback arrives. The organizational structure describes who can make decisions and how people communicate. A colocated team sits in one place. A virtual team is spread across locations or time zones. A hierarchical structure has one clear chain of command. A matrix structure has people reporting to both a functional manager, who controls their skills and staffing, and a project manager, who controls the work.

Predictive methods work when many people and suppliers need a stable baseline to build against. Written plans replace the daily conversations that colocated teams rely on. A clear authority line lets one person approve changes quickly.

Worked example: a regional hospital is replacing its scheduling system. Regulators fixed the required features. The IT department is hierarchical, so change approvals follow one line. An outside vendor in another region must build to written specifications. Step one: the scope is fixed by regulation. Step two: approvals flow one way. Step three: the vendor needs documents, not hallway talk. Conclusion: a predictive approach fits. Contrast this with a small colocated product team exploring a new app, where requirements are unknown and people talk every day. An adaptive approach fits there.

Common mistake: treating structure as the only factor, or assuming a virtual team must be adaptive. Structure is one input alongside fixed requirements, regulation and how stable the scope is. In a virtual team that runs without written agreements, members in different time zones form different understandings of the same requirement. Rework and missed dates follow. A predictive approach fits when the scope is stable and the structure can support written, controlled communication.

questions.prompt: A county water utility is replacing its meter-reading software. A state rule fixes the required billing fields, so the scope cannot change. The utility's IT office is hierarchical, so every change request goes to one IT director for approval. The software vendor is in another state and must build from written specifications. Step one: the scope is fixed by state rule. Step two: approvals flow through one line to the IT director. Step three: [missing]. Conclusion: a predictive approach fits.
choices: The vendor is in another state and works only from documents, so written, controlled specifications give it a stable baseline to build against.
Because the vendor is remote, the team should avoid any written agreements so it can adapt quickly.
The scope should stay open until the vendor delivers a prototype, then the utility decides the fields.
Daily stand-up calls are the best way to keep the vendor aligned with the utility.
questions.why: Step three must explain why written documents matter for a spread-out team, and only the choice that names a stable written baseline does that, matching how predictive methods replace daily conversation with plans.

questions.prompt: In a matrix structure, which statement correctly describes who controls what for a team member?
choices: The project manager controls the person's skills and staffing, and the functional manager controls the work.
The functional manager controls the work, and the person has no reporting line to anyone.
The person reports only to the project manager, who controls both skills and work.
The functional manager controls the person's skills and staffing, and the project manager controls the work.
questions.why: In a matrix, the functional manager controls skills and staffing while the project manager controls the work, which is the split described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A six-person team sits in one office at a logistics firm. They are building a new internal app, and the users have not yet decided what the app must do. The team talks every day. Which approach best fits, and why?
choices: Adaptive, because a virtual team is always better served by short cycles than by written plans.
Predictive, because a colocated team always needs a full written plan before starting any work.
Predictive, because the team sits in one office and can use one clear chain of command to approve all changes.
Adaptive, because requirements are unknown and daily conversation works well in a colocated team.
questions.why: With unknown requirements and a colocated team that talks daily, the teaching text says an adaptive approach fits, since written plans are not what keeps such a team aligned.

questions.prompt: A 12-person team is spread across three time zones to build a warehouse inventory tool. The client has signed a 40-page specification that is now frozen, and all change requests go to one approver who decides quickly. Which reasoning is the strongest?
choices: Because the team is virtual, it must be adaptive, so the frozen specification should be reopened every sprint.
Because the specification is stable and a single approver handles changes, a predictive approach fits, since written, controlled communication suits a spread-out team.
Because the team is spread out, any form of written plan is risky, so the team should rely on memory of verbal agreements.
Because the team is virtual, the approach is unclear, so the team should wait until everyone is in one room.
questions.why: A stable frozen scope plus a clear authority line and written communication is the situation where the teaching text says a predictive approach fits, even though the team is virtual.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a predictive, plan-based approach suits a project whose team is spread across three time zones and reports through a matrix. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the approach you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the scope. If the requirements are stable or fixed by a contract or regulation, a plan-based approach gives everyone a baseline to build against. The spread across three time zones pushes me toward a predictive approach as well, because people who rarely talk in real time need written plans and documented change requests. The matrix matters too: each person answers to a functional manager for staffing and a project manager for the work, so I would define one person who approves scope changes and write down who decides what. The tradeoff is that a plan-first approach is slow to absorb new information. If the requirements turn out to be uncertain, the approved baseline can lock the team into the wrong solution, so I would plan a formal change-control step to revisit the baseline when evidence changes.
rubricPoints: States that stable or fixed scope and a need for written, shared baselines favor a predictive approach
Connects virtual or distributed teams to the need for documented communication
Explains that matrix reporting requires clear decision rights for approving changes
Names a real limit, such as slow response to changing requirements or a locked-in baseline

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying an approach from structure and constraints is best practised by explaining the reasoning back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this decision.

lessons.plain: A predictive project is one where most of the plan is worked out early, before the main work starts, and the team then follows that plan while watching for drift. Think of building a house from blueprints: the architect fixes the rooms, the builder orders materials against a schedule, and any change goes through a formal request. Project management organizes this work into process groups, which are phases such as starting the project, planning it, carrying out the work, checking progress and correcting course, and closing it out. This objective asks you to know which activities belong to each group and which features a plan-first project tends to have, such as a fixed baseline and a formal change process.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is six weeks into a plan-first project when the client asks to add a new feature. Which kind of activity should handle that request, and why shouldn't the team simply add the feature to the work list?
lessons.teach:
A process group is a named phase of project management work. The five groups most often used are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. Each group contains activities, which are repeatable tasks that produce outputs such as a charter, a plan, a finished deliverable, a status report, or a final sign-off.

Why it works: in a predictive project, the team agrees on what done means before building begins. That agreement is called the baseline, a frozen reference for scope, schedule and cost. Once a baseline exists, progress can be measured against it, and any change must pass through change control, a formal step where a requested change is logged, assessed for its impact, and then approved or rejected.

Worked example: a team is upgrading a warehouse system. Initiating: they write a project charter that names the sponsor and the budget. Planning: they split the scope into a work breakdown structure, a tree of smaller deliverables, estimate durations, and set the baseline. Executing: the team builds and tests against the plan. Monitoring and controlling: each week they compare actual progress with the baseline and log any change request for review. Closing: they confirm acceptance with the client, release the team, and archive the records.

Common mistake: treating the plan as a one-time document rather than a baseline to monitor. Learners also place change approval under executing, when it belongs to monitoring and controlling.

In a running project, skipping change control lets scope creep in unnoticed. The baseline then stops meaning anything, and status reports show a false picture of health.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network is rolling out a new appointment system using a predictive approach. Initiating: the team writes a charter that names the sponsor and a budget of 80,000. Planning: they break the scope into a work breakdown structure of smaller deliverables, estimate durations, and freeze a baseline of 14 weeks. Executing: the team builds and tests the system against that plan. Monitoring and controlling: in week 6 a clinic manager asks for an extra reminder-text feature, and the team logs it as a change request and assesses its impact on the 14-week schedule and the budget. Step missing: the change request is then formally approved or rejected through change control before any work on it begins. Which choice correctly completes that missing step?
choices: The project manager quietly adds the feature to the plan so the status report stays accurate.
The request is archived with the closing records so it can be reviewed after go-live.
The team starts building the feature that week and updates the baseline at closing.
The request is approved or rejected through change control before any work begins, and the baseline changes only if it is approved.
questions.why: Change control is the formal step where a logged and assessed change is approved or rejected, and it has to happen before work on that change starts so the baseline stays meaningful.

questions.prompt: A project manager tells the sponsor that the baseline is now the agreed reference. Which description best matches what a baseline is?
choices: A frozen reference for scope, schedule and cost, agreed before building begins, against which progress is measured.
The final cost reported after the project has been closed out and archived.
A list of every person who has a role in the project, with their contact details.
A weekly status report listing which team members completed their tasks.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a baseline as a frozen reference for scope, schedule and cost agreed before building starts, which progress is measured against.

questions.prompt: A team on a predictive project is each week comparing actual progress against its frozen plan and logging any requested change for review. Which process group does this activity belong to?
choices: Initiating
Closing
Monitoring and controlling
Planning
questions.why: Comparing actual progress with the baseline and handling change requests are the monitoring and controlling activities, not initiating, planning or closing work.

questions.prompt: A small nonprofit's predictive project has a baseline, but the team treats the plan as a document written once at the start and never compares progress against it. Halfway through, the status report shows the project as on track while several unlogged extra features have been added. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Scope creep is caught early because the status report flags every new feature.
The project is closed early because the sponsor has no reason to keep funding it.
The baseline automatically updates to include the extra features, so the reports stay accurate.
The status reports give a false picture of health because the baseline no longer means anything.
questions.why: Without monitoring against the baseline and change control, unlogged additions creep in and the status reports show a misleading picture, as the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how the process groups of a predictive project differ from one another, and name one limit of relying on a fixed baseline.
lessons.modelAnswer: The groups follow the project's life in order. Initiating authorizes the project and names the sponsor and budget. Planning turns the scope into a breakdown of deliverables, a schedule, a cost estimate and the baseline. Executing produces the deliverables. Monitoring and controlling compares actual progress with the baseline each period and runs change requests through a formal review. Closing confirms acceptance and archives the records. The main limit of a fixed baseline is that it assumes the early plan is roughly right. If the client's needs or the environment shift, the baseline can become outdated, and every change adds paperwork and delay, so the team may keep reporting against a plan nobody believes in.
rubricPoints: Names the five process groups in their normal order
Explains that the baseline is the agreed reference for scope, schedule and cost
Places change control within monitoring and controlling
States a real limit, such as an outdated baseline or slow change approval

suggested.rationale: Naming the groups and sorting activities into them is recall of a framework, which reading and self-checking covers better than any listed mission or engine.

lessons.plain: Some projects have a chain of tasks where a delay in any one of them pushes the finish date back. The critical path is the longest such chain of dependent tasks through the project, and it sets the shortest possible total duration. Tasks off that chain have some slack, meaning they can slip a little without moving the end date. Schedule variance is a simple progress check: it compares the work you have actually finished, measured in budgeted value, with the work you planned to have finished by now. A negative result means you are behind schedule. Together these ideas show which delays matter and whether the project is on track.
lessons.guessPrompt: Task A takes 1 day. Task B takes 2 days and can start only after A finishes. Task C takes 5 days and can also start only after A finishes. Task D takes 1 day and needs both B and C to be finished before it starts. Which of the two middle tasks, B or C, do you think controls how soon the project can finish, and why?
lessons.teach:
An activity is a piece of planned work with a duration. A dependency is a rule that one activity must finish before another can start. A network is the set of activities linked by their dependencies. The critical path method, or CPM, finds the longest chain of dependent activities from start to finish. That chain is the critical path, and its total duration is the shortest the project can take, because nothing on it can run in parallel to save time.

CPM works in two passes. A forward pass adds durations along each route to get each activity's earliest start and earliest finish. A backward pass starts from the end and works back to get latest finish and latest start. Float, also called slack, is latest finish minus earliest finish. Activities with zero float lie on the critical path. A delay there moves the end date; a delay in an activity with float does not, until the float is used up.

Worked example: A takes 1 day. B takes 2 days and needs A. C takes 5 days and needs A. D takes 1 day and needs both B and C. Route A-B-D totals 4 days; route A-C-D totals 7 days. The critical path is A-C-D, 7 days. B can finish as late as day 6 without delaying D, so B has 2 days of float.

Schedule variance, or SV, checks progress against the plan. Planned value, PV, is the budgeted value of work scheduled to be complete by a given date. Earned value, EV, is the budgeted value of work actually complete. SV equals EV minus PV. Suppose there are 20 equal deliverables, each worth one unit of budget. At week 6 the plan calls for 12 complete, so PV is 12. If 9 are complete, EV is 9 and SV is -3, meaning the project is behind schedule. SV uses budgeted value, not money spent, so it measures time progress rather than cost.

Common mistake: treating the critical path as the set of the most important or most expensive tasks. It depends only on durations and dependencies, and it changes when those change.

Consequence: a team that works hard on B because it looks busy, while C slips a day, pushes the finish date back a day and may not notice until late.

CPM shows where a delay will actually hurt, and SV shows whether the project is keeping pace.

questions.prompt: A small office relocation has four activities. Pack boxes takes 3 days and has no dependency. Move furniture takes 2 days and needs Pack boxes to be finished first. Book internet installation takes 4 days and has no dependency. Connect internet takes 1 day and needs both Move furniture and Book internet to be finished first. The forward pass gives Pack boxes an earliest finish of day 3, Move furniture day 5, Book internet day 4, and Connect internet day 6, so the project takes 6 days. Connect internet must start no later than day 5 to keep the 6-day finish, so Book internet must finish no later than day 5. Step left for you: using float equals latest finish minus earliest finish, what is the float of Book internet installation?
choices: 4 days
0 days
2 days
1 day
questions.why: Book internet has a latest finish of day 5 and an earliest finish of day 4, so 5 minus 4 gives 1 day of float.

questions.prompt: A bakery opening has these activities: Design menu, 2 days. Source equipment, 6 days. Hire staff, 3 days, needs Design menu finished. Install equipment, 2 days, needs Source equipment finished. Train staff, 2 days, needs Hire staff and Install equipment both finished. What is the length of the critical path?
choices: 7 days
6 days
15 days
10 days
questions.why: The longest chain is Source equipment, Install equipment, Train staff, totalling 6 + 2 + 2 = 10 days, while the chain through Design menu and Hire staff totals only 7 days and the 15-day figure is the sum of every activity, which CPM does not use.

questions.prompt: A software project's critical path is 9 days long. A design review takes 3 days and has 2 days of float. The review slips by 2 days. What happens to the project end date?
choices: The end date moves 1 day later
The end date moves 4 days later because the slip doubles
The end date is unchanged, since the slip uses the float exactly
The end date moves 2 days later
questions.why: Activities with float can absorb delays up to the size of their float, so a 2-day slip against 2 days of float leaves the critical path and the end date unchanged.

questions.prompt: A website redesign is split into 30 test cases, each worth one unit of budget. At week 4 the plan calls for 18 cases to be passed, and the team has passed 15. What is the schedule variance, and what does it mean?
choices: +3, meaning behind schedule
-3, meaning over budget because spending is higher than planned
+3, meaning ahead of schedule
-3, meaning behind schedule
questions.why: SV equals EV minus PV, so 15 minus 18 gives -3, and a negative SV means the project is behind its planned progress, measured in budgeted value rather than money spent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the critical path is, how it differs from float, and one limit of using schedule variance alone to judge a project.
lessons.modelAnswer: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish, and its total duration is the shortest the project can take. Tasks on it have zero float, so any delay there moves the end date. Float is how far a task can slip without moving the finish; a task with float can run late without hurting the end, up to that amount. A limit of schedule variance is that it only uses the budgeted value of completed work, so a negative SV tells you we are behind but not why, and not whether the remaining work has now moved onto the critical path. It also depends on how the work was valued at the start, so a weak original estimate distorts it. I would check the critical path and float before deciding where to send people, and use SV as a signal to investigate rather than as a diagnosis.
rubricPoints: Defines the critical path as the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the shortest possible duration.
Explains float as slack that lets a task slip without moving the end date, and zero float as marking the critical path.
Calculates schedule variance as earned value minus planned value and reads a negative result as behind schedule.
States a limit, such as SV reflecting budgeted value and original estimates rather than the root cause of a delay.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises critical path or variance, so an exam-style scenario to reason through adds the most.

lessons.plain: A work breakdown structure, usually shortened to WBS, is a family tree that splits a big project into smaller pieces, from the top down, until each piece is small enough to plan, assign, and check. Think of planning a family wedding. You would not write 'run the wedding' as one line. You would split it into venue, catering, invitations, and so on, then keep splitting until each piece has a clear owner and a clear finish. The smallest pieces at the bottom of the tree are called work packages. A good tree means nothing important is forgotten and everyone knows what done looks like.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must plan a school fundraising event with 40 volunteers. Would you start by listing what the finished event must include, such as venue, food, tickets, and cleanup, or by listing this week's tasks? Explain your choice in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A work breakdown structure, or WBS, is a hierarchy that breaks the total scope of a project into smaller parts. Scope means all the work needed to deliver the project's results. Decomposition means splitting a part into its own parts. The top element is the whole project. Each element below it is a child of the element above, and splitting continues until an element is small enough to estimate, schedule, assign to one owner, and check for completion. The lowest elements are work packages, the units of work that are actually planned, costed, and tracked. Elements are usually named as deliverables, which are tangible results such as a report or a built component, rather than as activities, because results stay stable when the plan changes.

Why it works: people estimate a small, concrete piece far more accurately than a vague whole. The 100% rule says each level must contain all the work of its parent, no more and no less.

Worked example: a school fundraiser. Level 1 is the fundraiser. Level 2 has four children: venue, food, tickets, and cleanup. Under tickets, Level 3 has design ticket, print 300 tickets, sell tickets, and reconcile cash. Each of those is a work package with one owner and a finish condition, such as 'print 300 tickets: 300 printed tickets delivered to the front office'. Check the rule: the four Level 2 items together cover the whole event, and the four Level 3 items together cover tickets.

Common mistake: stopping too early, leaving food as one large package, or organizing the tree by phases such as design, build, and test instead of results. Another mistake is never writing down what each package means, so two people read it differently. A WBS dictionary, which is a short written description of each element, prevents this.

Consequence: if a deliverable is missing from the WBS, its work is never scheduled or budgeted, and it appears late as an unplanned surprise. A WBS organizes the work; it does not by itself show the order of work or the dates.

questions.prompt: A bakery is adding online ordering. Level 1 is the online ordering launch. Level 2 has four children: storefront website, payment handling, pickup and delivery, and staff training. Under payment handling, Level 3 has three packages: choose a card processor, build the checkout page, and set up the refund process. The one step not yet done is to add the Level 3 package that covers the remaining payment work, so that the payment handling items together cover all payment handling. Which finish condition fits that missing package?
choices: Payment team meets weekly to discuss processor options
Daily card settlements matched to bank deposits, with gaps listed in a report to the owner
Website launched on the public domain by the opening date
Refund process scheduled for week three
questions.why: The missing package must be a deliverable under payment handling with a checkable finish condition, and daily settlement matching is payment work not yet covered, while the other choices are a meeting, a work in another branch, and a schedule date rather than a finish condition.

questions.prompt: In a work breakdown structure, which description best fits a work package?
choices: The lowest-level element that is planned, costed, and tracked, with one owner and a finish condition
The top element of the tree that names the whole project
A calendar showing when each task starts and ends
A phase label such as design, build, or test that groups several tasks
questions.why: A work package is defined in the teaching text as the lowest element that is planned, costed, and tracked, and it needs one owner and a clear finish condition.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's WBS for a warehouse expansion has three children under the warehouse: Phase 1 Planning, Phase 2 Build, and Phase 3 Testing. What is the main problem with this structure?
choices: Three children is too few, so the tree must have at least five branches to be valid
The branches are organized by phases instead of by deliverables, which is a common mistake that makes results unclear
Phase names are acceptable, but the team should add calendar dates to each one
The warehouse should be removed from Level 1 and replaced with a list of tasks
questions.why: The teaching text warns against organizing the tree by phases such as design, build, and test rather than by results, and the deliverables should be named instead.

questions.prompt: A school library renovation has a Level 2 parent with four children: shelving, lighting, flooring, and furniture. During planning, the team realizes painting the walls is not in any branch. What does the 100% rule say to do?
choices: Leave painting out, since the four items already describe the renovation
Add painting as a child under the renovation so the Level 2 items again cover all renovation work
Move painting to Level 1 as a separate project
Make painting a work package under flooring because both involve surfaces
questions.why: The 100% rule requires each level to contain all the work of its parent, so painting must be placed as a child of the renovation to keep the children complete.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never built a WBS how to turn a vague deliverable such as 'the new website' into work packages, and name one limit or tradeoff of how far you should decompose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start from the top: the new website is the single top element. Ask what the finished site must contain as tangible results, such as the home page, the product catalogue, the checkout, and the hosting setup, and make each one a child element. Keep splitting each child until a piece has one owner, a clear finished state, and an estimate someone can give, such as 'checkout payment form tested with three test cards'. Those bottom pieces are the work packages. The tradeoff is depth. Stop too early and the pieces are too big to estimate or track, so surprises hide inside them. Go too deep and the WBS becomes slow to maintain, with many tiny items that add overhead without better control. A reasonable stopping point is a package that can be reported as done or not done within a normal reporting period, often one to two weeks of effort.
rubricPoints: Starts from the whole project and decomposes top-down into deliverables.
Defines a work package as the lowest planned element, with one owner and a clear finish.
Applies the 100% rule: each level covers all the work of its parent, no more and no less.
Gives a stopping rule: decompose until an element is estimable, assignable, and checkable.
Names the tradeoff between decomposing too shallowly and too deeply.

suggested.rationale: Decomposing a scenario and checking that the children cover the parent is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, which no listed mission or planned engine currently provides.

lessons.plain: In a plan-driven project, the team agrees on a detailed plan up front and then steers toward it. The written records that make this possible are called artifacts. One document says why the project exists, one says what work is in scope, one holds the agreed dates and budget, and others record problems, risks, and every change someone asks for. Think of them as the paperwork of a bridge being built: the blueprint, the schedule, and the sign-off sheets. Knowing which document holds which kind of information tells you where to look when something goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: Partway through a project, a sponsor asks for an extra feature. Which document should record that request, and which agreed document should you check to see whether it moves the finish date?
lessons.teach:
An artifact is any document or record a project produces to describe the work or track it. In a predictive project, a few artifacts do most of the controlling. The project charter is the short document that formally authorizes the project and names the project manager and main objectives. The work breakdown structure, or WBS, is a hierarchy that splits total scope into smaller pieces of deliverable work; its lowest pieces are called work packages. A baseline is an approved version of a plan, such as the schedule baseline or cost baseline, kept fixed so later performance can be measured against it. The change log records every requested change, its estimated impact on scope, schedule, and cost, and the decision made. The issue log holds current problems, and the risk register holds possible future events and how they are being handled.

Why it works: the baseline gives a fixed yardstick, and the change log makes every movement away from that yardstick visible and approved rather than silent.

Worked example: a team fitting out a data centre has an approved schedule baseline with cabling finishing on day 40. A stakeholder asks for extra power outlets. The team raises a change request, estimates that cabling now needs 3 more days, and the control board approves it. The change log records the request, the estimate, and the decision, and a new schedule version is saved as baseline 2 while baseline 1 is kept for reporting. When a later slip appears, it is measured against the correct yardstick.

Common mistake: editing the baseline in place when a change is agreed informally. The original plan then disappears, and variance reports look as if nothing moved.

Consequence: the operations team cannot tell whether a late cutover came from a real delay or from a quietly accepted scope addition, so they cannot decide what to fix.

Controlled documents make the project's history explainable, and that history is the only evidence a steering group has.

questions.prompt: A regional library network is consolidating three branch catalogues into one system. The approved schedule baseline has the migration finishing in week 12. A branch manager asks for barcode scanning at the front desk. The team estimates the scanning work adds 2 weeks, and the control board approves the request. The team records the request, the 2-week estimate, and the approval in the change log. The team then saves the revised schedule as a new baseline version. Step left out: the earlier baseline is kept unchanged for reporting, so the approved change can be shown against it. What should happen to the earlier baseline at this point?
choices: It is kept unchanged for reporting, so later performance can be compared with the original plan.
It is moved into the issue log as a current problem until the migration finishes.
It is deleted, since the change log already holds the full record of the change.
It is overwritten with the new dates so the schedule shows only one version.
questions.why: Keeping the earlier baseline unchanged preserves the fixed yardstick, which lets later slips be measured against the original plan rather than the revised one.

questions.prompt: Which artifact holds possible future events that might affect the project, along with how the team plans to respond to each one?
choices: The issue log
The risk register
The change log
The project charter
questions.why: The risk register holds possible future events and their handling, whereas the issue log holds problems that already exist.

questions.prompt: A software team quietly adjusts the approved cost baseline in place after an informal agreement with a sponsor, with no change request raised. What is the most likely consequence for later variance reporting?
choices: The variance reports show the original cost plan as the reference point, so the overrun is highlighted.
The original plan disappears, so variance reports can look as if nothing moved and the real cause of a slip is hidden.
The variance reports flag the change clearly as an approved scope addition.
The change log automatically reconstructs the original baseline for comparison.
questions.why: Editing the baseline in place removes the original yardstick, so reports show no movement and the team cannot tell whether a slip came from real delay or an accepted addition.

questions.prompt: A team planning a website launch splits the total scope into smaller pieces of deliverable work, and the smallest pieces are the units that get assigned and tracked. What is the term for these smallest pieces in a work breakdown structure?
choices: Work package
Project charter
Issue
Baseline
questions.why: In a WBS, the lowest-level pieces of deliverable work are called work packages, while baselines, charters, and issues are different artifacts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which artifacts you would check first when a predictive project's finish date slips, and name one limit of relying on those documents.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the schedule baseline to confirm the agreed finish date and the planned dates for the affected work packages. Then I would check the change log for approved changes since the baseline that may already have moved those dates. Next I would look at the issue log for open blockers and the risk register to see whether a listed risk has occurred. Comparing actual progress from status reports against the baseline shows where the slip started. One limit is that these documents are only as current as the people updating them. If status reports are stale or a change was agreed verbally and never logged, the records will look cleaner than reality, so I would confirm with the people doing the work before concluding anything.
rubricPoints: Names the schedule baseline as the agreed reference for dates
Explains that the change log shows approved changes that may have moved dates
Mentions the issue log and risk register as sources of blockers or occurred risks
States a real limit, such as stale or unlogged information in the records

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises identifying project control artifacts, so reading the definitions and their roles is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: Project control data is the set of numbers that show how a plan is really going: what was supposed to be done by now, what is actually done, and what has been spent. A variance is the gap between a planned number and a real one. Schedule variance shows whether work is running ahead of or behind the calendar, and cost variance shows whether money is going further or faster than planned. Working out these gaps lets a project manager spot trouble early, while there is still time to act, instead of finding out at the end when the deadline or budget has already slipped.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project was budgeted to have finished 50 percent of its work by today, but it has finished only 30 percent. It has also spent more money than its budget says it should have by now. Without using any formulas, what two separate problems is this project facing, and which one would you raise first with the sponsor?
lessons.teach:
Three numbers drive this. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted value of the work scheduled to be finished by a given date. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted value of the work actually completed so far. Actual cost (AC) is the money actually spent to get that work done. All three are measured at the same point in time, called the status date.

Two variances follow from them. Schedule variance (SV) equals EV minus PV. Cost variance (CV) equals EV minus AC. A negative number is a warning: negative SV means the project is behind schedule, and negative CV means it is over budget. A positive number means ahead of schedule or under budget.

Why it works: EV is the anchor. It states what the completed work is worth at the budgeted rate, so it can be compared fairly with both the plan (PV) and the bill (AC). Comparing AC with PV alone mixes up spending with progress.

Worked example: a project has a total budget of 50,000 over 10 weeks. At week 4 the plan says 40 percent of the work should be done, so PV is 20,000. The team has finished 30 percent of the work, so EV is 15,000. They have spent 18,000, so AC is 18,000. Step one: SV = 15,000 minus 20,000, which is minus 5,000, so the project is behind. Step two: CV = 15,000 minus 18,000, which is minus 3,000, so the project is over budget. The team has spent close to what the plan expected for this point, yet delivered less work than planned.

Common mistake: treating spending that matches the plan as proof of health. Spending 20,000 against a plan of 20,000 looks fine until you notice that only 15,000 of value has been earned.

In a running project the consequence is a forecast that drifts. If both variances stay negative across several status dates, the completion date and final cost will slip unless scope or resources change.

questions.prompt: A community kitchen build has a total budget of 80,000 over 12 weeks. At the status date in week 6, the plan says 50 percent of the work should be finished, so PV is 40,000. The crew has finished 35 percent of the work, so EV is 28,000. They have spent 30,000, so AC is 30,000. Step one: SV = 28,000 minus 40,000, which is minus 12,000, so the build is behind schedule. Step two: CV = ____. Fill in the missing step.
choices: CV = 40,000 minus 30,000, which is plus 10,000, so the build is under budget
CV = 28,000 minus 40,000, which is minus 12,000, so the build is behind schedule
CV = 30,000 minus 28,000, which is plus 2,000, so the build is under budget
CV = 28,000 minus 30,000, which is minus 2,000, so the build is over budget
questions.why: Cost variance is EV minus AC, so 28,000 minus 30,000 gives minus 2,000, and a negative value means the project is over budget.

questions.prompt: A status report says the project is on budget because the money spent so far (AC) equals the amount the plan expected to be spent by now (PV). Which statement best identifies the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: The reasoning is fine because AC and PV are the only two numbers needed to judge cost
Matching spend to the plan proves the schedule is also on track, so no other check is needed
PV should be replaced by the total project budget before any comparison is made
Spending that matches the plan does not show how much work was completed, so EV must be compared with AC
questions.why: Earned value is the anchor that measures completed work, and without it the spend figure cannot show whether the money bought the planned progress.

questions.prompt: A server migration is checked at a status date. Planned value is 90,000, earned value is 84,000, and actual cost is 96,000. What are the schedule variance and cost variance?
choices: SV is plus 6,000 and CV is plus 12,000, so the migration is ahead and under budget
SV is minus 6,000 and CV is plus 12,000, so the migration is behind but under budget
SV is minus 12,000 and CV is minus 6,000, so the migration is behind and slightly over budget
SV is minus 6,000 and CV is minus 12,000, so the migration is behind and over budget
questions.why: SV is EV minus PV, which is 84,000 minus 90,000 equals minus 6,000, and CV is EV minus AC, which is 84,000 minus 96,000 equals minus 12,000, so both are negative.

questions.prompt: A project manager sees negative schedule variance and negative cost variance on three status dates in a row. A team member says the numbers will recover on their own once spending catches up with the plan. According to the predictive method's logic, what is the most likely outcome if nothing about scope or resources changes?
choices: The variances are a one-time reporting error and will vanish at the next status date
The project will finish early because negative variances show the team is overestimating work
The completion date and final cost are likely to slip, because the forecast drifts while both variances stay negative
The variances will correct themselves once spending matches planned value, so no forecast change is needed
questions.why: The teaching text says that when both variances stay negative across several status dates, the forecast drifts and completion and final cost slip unless scope or resources change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a project is over budget and behind schedule, using planned value, earned value and actual cost, and name one limit of these variance figures.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would take three numbers at the same status date: planned value, the budgeted value of the work scheduled to be done by now; earned value, the budgeted value of the work actually done; and actual cost, what we have spent. Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value. If it is negative, we are behind the calendar. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost. If it is negative, we are over budget. I would present both together, because a project can be on schedule yet overspent, or under budget yet late. One limit is that these figures are only as good as the progress estimate behind earned value. If the team overstates percent complete, both variances look better than reality. Another limit is that each figure is a snapshot, so the trend across several status dates tells you more than one negative number.
rubricPoints: Defines planned value, earned value and actual cost at the same status date
Computes schedule variance as earned value minus planned value and cost variance as earned value minus actual cost
Reads a negative variance as behind schedule or over budget
Names a limit such as dependence on accurate percent-complete estimates
Notes that the trend across several status dates matters more than a single snapshot

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style status scenario with several competing numbers adds more than any listed mission, since none of them practise earned value.

lessons.plain: Choosing between an adaptive and a predictive approach means deciding how a project should be planned and changed. A predictive approach plans most of the work up front, fixes the scope, and then carries it out in order, much like designing a building before construction starts. An adaptive approach expects the plan to change, so it delivers work in short cycles and adjusts based on what the team and customers learn along the way, like tasting a dish as you cook it. The skill is noticing which conditions make one approach the safer bet: how well the needs are understood, how much the customer is likely to change their mind, how the organization is structured, and what past projects have taught the company.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new feature whose future users have never been asked what they want, and the business expects the idea to change after the first demo. Would you plan the whole thing up front or deliver it in short cycles, and why?
lessons.teach:
A predictive approach, sometimes called plan-driven or waterfall, front-loads requirements, scope, schedule and cost, then executes the work in sequence. An adaptive approach, which includes agile methods, accepts that requirements will shift, so it delivers work in short time-boxed cycles and reviews results with stakeholders before deciding what comes next. Two kinds of inputs guide the choice. Enterprise environmental factors (EEFs) are conditions outside the project team's control, such as market volatility, regulations, contract types, organizational culture, and the skills available. Organizational process assets (OPAs) are what the organization has built internally: policies, templates, lessons learned, and historical data showing how earlier projects actually went.

Adaptive methods pay off when uncertainty is high and building the wrong thing costs more than revisiting the plan. Short cycles expose wrong assumptions early, while changing course is still cheap. Predictive methods pay off when requirements are stable, the deliverable is fixed by regulation or contract, and each change must pass a formal approval.

Organizational structure matters too. Adaptive work needs a team that can make decisions close to the work, with a product owner or customer reachable most days. A rigid hierarchy with many sign-off gates, or a team split across several vendors on fixed-price contracts, pushes toward predictive.

Worked example. A dispatch software team is adding a driver-notification feature. Step 1: nobody yet knows the exact rules drivers want. Step 2: the product owner sits with the team daily. Step 3: leadership accepts changes after each demo. Step 4: the company's past projects show short cycles worked well. Result: adaptive fits.

Common mistake. Choosing adaptive because it sounds modern, without checking the environment. If the contract fixes scope and a regulator must approve one final document, short cycles create rework and approval conflicts.

Consequence. Adaptive delivery in a fixed-scope, regulated setting can leave a half-approved release running in production, while predictive planning in a volatile market can ship a feature nobody wants months late. The right question is which conditions this project actually has.

questions.prompt: A municipal library is replacing its book-return kiosk software. Its procurement rules require a fixed-price vendor contract with one signed scope document before any build starts, which is an enterprise environmental factor the team cannot change. The library's own records (an organizational process asset) show that three earlier kiosk projects were each delayed when mid-build changes waited for the quarterly finance committee. Step 1: the contract fixes scope and needs one signed document. Step 2: each change must wait for a quarterly committee vote. Step 3: [missing step]. Result: predictive fits.
choices: Confirm the decision path: changes route through several sign-off gates, so decisions are not made close to the work, which points toward predictive.
Ask the vendor which method it prefers and adopt that method without further checks.
Assume adaptive is right because the library wants a modern, user-friendly kiosk.
Count how many sprints the library's last kiosk project used, and choose whatever number is closest to that.
questions.why: A rigid approval chain with several gates and no decision-maker near the work is the organizational-structure signal that pushes toward predictive, so that is the missing check.

questions.prompt: A seed-bank software firm is starting a new inventory project. Which item is an organizational process asset rather than an enterprise environmental factor?
choices: A lessons-learned log from the firm's last three launches that records where schedules slipped
The local shortage of database engineers that makes hiring slow in the area
The firm's culture of open-plan seating and frequent informal meetings
Regional export rules that limit how seed samples may be shipped across state lines
questions.why: A lessons-learned log is something the organization built internally from past projects, which makes it an organizational process asset; the other three are conditions outside the team's control, so they are enterprise environmental factors.

questions.prompt: A regional ferry operator must have its booking-system change approved by a transport regulator through one signed final safety document before deployment, and the contract fixes scope. A team proposes releasing a partial booking module every two weeks with stakeholder demos. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The stakeholders will reject every demo, so the team will never finish any part of the work.
Partial releases will collide with the one-document approval rule, creating rework and approval conflicts.
The cycles will let the team plan dependencies too early, which will push the schedule out.
The team will spend too little time on documentation, which the regulator is likely to praise.
questions.why: Short cycles can leave half-approved releases that conflict with a rule requiring a single final approved document, which is the failure case the teaching text warns about in fixed-scope, regulated settings.

questions.prompt: Which combination of conditions most strongly favors an adaptive approach for a new fitness-app feature?
choices: A regulator-approved final document, a vendor team on fixed-price terms, and quarterly change votes
A scope fixed by a signed contract, a notarized specification, and one approval per year
Stable requirements, with every change needing a formal committee review before work resumes
Uncertain user preferences, a product owner reachable most days, and past short cycles that worked well
questions.why: High uncertainty, a reachable decision-maker, and an organizational history of successful short cycles are the conditions the teaching text associates with adaptive methods.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether a project should be adaptive or predictive, including one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how certain the requirements are and how costly a late change would be. If the customer's needs are unclear and they will likely react to early results, an adaptive approach fits, because short cycles surface wrong assumptions while changing course is still cheap. Next I check the environment and the organization: is the product owner reachable, can the team make decisions without many sign-offs, and do the company's past projects show that iterative delivery worked? If the scope is fixed by a contract or a regulator needs one approved document, predictive is safer. The tradeoff with adaptive is that the final scope and total cost are less certain up front, so stakeholders need to accept that they will steer the work through reviews. If they cannot accept that, I would not choose adaptive, even when the requirements are unclear.
rubricPoints: Adaptive fits when requirements are uncertain and change is expected, because short cycles expose wrong assumptions early.
Predictive fits when scope is fixed by contract or regulation and changes require formal approval.
Organizational structure matters: adaptive needs empowered, co-located or reachable decision-makers and a product owner.
EEFs and OPAs such as market conditions, culture, and lessons learned from past projects should inform the choice.
A real tradeoff of adaptive is less up-front certainty about final scope, cost, and schedule.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an approach from the surrounding conditions is a judgment skill best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission teaches this selection directly.

lessons.plain: When a team works in short, fixed-length chunks of time, each chunk is called an iteration. Planning iterations means deciding how to slice a big body of work into those chunks and what goes into each one. A work breakdown structure, or WBS, is a tree that splits a project into deliverables and then into smaller pieces. Turning that tree into iterations means choosing which pieces can be finished, tested, and shown together in one chunk. Good slicing gives the team something real to review at the end of each chunk, so they can change direction early instead of at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A WBS branch called 'Alert system' has three pieces: store the alert rules, send the notifications, and show a dashboard. If you can only finish one piece per two-week iteration, which order would you choose and why?
lessons.teach:
An iteration is a fixed time box, often one to four weeks, in which a team builds and finishes a set of work. A time box is a set length of time that does not stretch; the scope inside it is what gets adjusted. A logical iteration unit is the rule you use to decide what counts as one iteration's worth of work. Common units are a fixed time box (every iteration is the same length and the scope flexes to fit), a feature slice (one complete capability a user can check), and a milestone (a whole WBS branch finished at once). A work package is the smallest item in the WBS, the leaf that someone can actually do.

Why it works: a fixed time box keeps the rhythm predictable and makes pace measurable, while a complete slice of value gives feedback early. To translate a WBS, group the work packages that together produce something testable, then order the groups so prerequisites come first and the most valuable outcomes come early.

Worked example: the alert branch has three packages, and the team has two-week iterations. Step 1: rule storage alone produces nothing a user can check. Step 2: they group rule storage with a basic notification send, so one alert can be created and delivered end to end. Step 3: the dashboard moves to iteration 2. Each iteration now ends with something demonstrable.

Common mistake: slicing by WBS layer, with all design in iteration 1, all build in iteration 2, and all testing in iteration 3. Nothing is usable until the end, so feedback arrives too late.

Consequence: in a running system, a layer-based plan means the first working alert appears only after the final iteration, and defects found then are expensive to fix. Slicing by complete value keeps the system demonstrable throughout the project.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling team has a WBS branch called appointment reminders with four work packages: write the reminder message template, set up the SMS gateway account, build the opt-out handling, and build the reminder scheduler. They run three-week fixed time boxes. Step 1: the message template alone produces nothing a patient can receive, so it cannot be an iteration on its own. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: opt-out handling is moved to iteration 2 because it is valuable but only matters once reminders already reach patients.
choices: Keep all four packages in iteration 1 because the appointment reminders branch is one milestone and must finish together
Group the template, the gateway setup and the scheduler into iteration 1 so one reminder can be created and sent end to end to a test phone
Move the SMS gateway account setup to iteration 3 so that all infrastructure is finished last
Put each work package into its own iteration so that every leaf of the WBS is a separate unit
questions.why: Step 2 should group the packages that together produce one reminder that can be checked end to end, which is the complete slice the teaching text describes, while the other options either delay that slice, treat a whole branch as one unit, or treat single leaves as units.

questions.prompt: In a fixed time box approach, which element is allowed to change when the team runs short of time in an iteration?
choices: The length of the iteration, which is extended by a week
The team size, which is increased for the final days
The deadline for the whole project, which is moved back
The scope of work included in the iteration, which is adjusted to fit the time
questions.why: A time box is a set length that does not stretch, so the work inside it is what gets adjusted to fit.

questions.prompt: A data team plans iteration 1 as only the schema design for a reporting module: the tables and column definitions, with no screens, queries or reports yet. Why is this a weak iteration unit under the logical iteration rules?
choices: It produces nothing a user can check, so it does not give early feedback on a complete capability
Schema work should always be placed in the final iteration of a project
Iterations must contain at least five work packages to be valid
Schema design is always a work package and so cannot appear inside an iteration
questions.why: A logical iteration unit should group packages that together produce something testable, and a schema alone gives a user nothing to check, so feedback arrives late.

questions.prompt: A product team wants to measure how much work it completes each iteration so it can predict future pace. One candidate unit is a milestone, meaning a whole WBS branch finished at once. What is the main drawback of choosing milestones as the iteration unit for this goal?
choices: Milestones cannot be placed in any order, so prerequisites are ignored
Milestones make the iteration length vary with the branch size, so the pace is harder to compare from one iteration to the next
Milestones always produce more defects than feature slices
Milestones remove the need for a work package breakdown
questions.why: A fixed time box keeps the rhythm predictable and makes pace measurable, whereas milestone-sized units change in length, which makes pace harder to compare.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn one WBS branch into iterations, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the leaf work packages under the branch and ask which ones together produce something a user or tester can check. I would group those into one iteration, then order the groups so prerequisites come first and the most valuable outcome comes early. I would keep the iteration length fixed, so the team's pace is measurable, and let the scope inside each iteration flex. The tradeoff is that a value slice can leave some technical groundwork incomplete for a while, so I would flag any shared foundation work as its own explicit item, and I would accept that the first iteration may look thin to stakeholders who expect everything at once.
rubricPoints: Groups work packages by what can be finished and checked together, not by WBS layer or discipline
Keeps iteration length fixed and lets scope flex, or explains a clear alternative logical unit
Orders groups by dependency and by value to the customer
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as thin early iterations or foundation work that is harder to slot in

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through a WBS-to-iteration translation and justifying it aloud, which an explanation exercise tests better than a console task.

lessons.plain: When a project team plans its work, it needs to know what goes into the work and how it will check progress. In a predictive project, the team agrees on the full scope up front, measures progress against that fixed plan, and handles changes through a formal review. In an adaptive project, the team starts with a prioritized list of wanted outcomes, plans only the next short slice of work, and checks progress by looking at what has actually been finished and what remains. The list gets updated as the team learns. Think of a road trip with a fixed destination and a route printed in advance, compared with one where you plan the next town and adjust as you go.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a mobile app and the customer keeps changing their mind about features. Which would you expect to change more: the total scope written at the start, or the order of the next few features to build? Why?
lessons.teach:
Scope is the set of work a project will deliver. Scope inputs are the information a team uses to decide what belongs in that set. In a predictive project these inputs are a charter, a requirements document, and a work breakdown structure (WBS), which is a hierarchy that splits deliverables into smaller pieces of work. Together they form a scope baseline, an agreed reference that progress is measured against. Tracking then compares planned value with earned value, the planned worth of the work actually completed, and any change goes through formal change control. In an adaptive project the main scope input is a product backlog, an ordered list of wanted outcomes, usually written as user stories, which are short statements of what a user needs and why. Each story has acceptance criteria, the conditions that show it is finished. The team also shares a definition of done, a checklist every finished item must meet. Work is pulled into a time-boxed iteration, a fixed-length cycle, by priority rather than fixed up front.

Worked example: a backlog holds 60 story points, a rough size measure. Iteration 1 finishes 15 points and iteration 2 finishes 18. Remaining work is 27 points. The average of about 16 points per iteration suggests roughly two more iterations if the backlog does not change. A burndown chart plots remaining points against iterations, so the team can see the trend and reorder the backlog when priorities shift.

Common mistake: counting partly built stories as done, or treating the first estimate as a contract. That makes the burndown look healthier than the product really is.

Consequence: a predictive team that skips change control loses its baseline, while an adaptive team that counts only finished, accepted items gets an honest forecast that moves as it learns. Adaptive tracking asks where the work stands now, not whether it still matches the original plan.

questions.prompt: A payments support team has a product backlog of 90 story points, where a story point is a rough size measure of work. Iteration 1 finishes 20 accepted points, iteration 2 finishes 22, and iteration 3 finishes 18. Step one is done: 60 points are finished, 30 remain, and the team has averaged 20 points per iteration. If the backlog does not change, which step completes the forecast?
choices: Add the 60 finished points to the 30 remaining to confirm the 90-point total, then stop because the forecast is already fixed.
Treat the original 90-point estimate as a contract and assume the team will finish in exactly three iterations.
Divide the 30 remaining points by the 20-point average to get 1.5, so plan for about two more iterations.
Count the 12 partly built points as finished so the remaining work falls to 18, then assume one more iteration.
questions.why: Dividing remaining work by the recent average gives a forecast that can be revised, while the other options either count unfinished work, treat an estimate as fixed, or restate totals without forecasting.

questions.prompt: In an adaptive project, what is an acceptance criterion?
choices: The specific conditions that show one user story is finished.
A team-wide checklist that every finished item must meet, such as review and testing steps agreed in advance.
A fixed date by which an iteration must end, set before the iteration starts.
The ordered list of all wanted outcomes that the product owner keeps up to date.
questions.why: Acceptance criteria are the conditions for a single story, whereas the definition of done is the shared checklist and the backlog is the ordered list of outcomes.

questions.prompt: During an iteration, a developer has finished coding a story but its testing is not complete and its acceptance criteria are not yet met. How should the team count this story on the burndown chart?
choices: Count it at 80 percent so the chart reflects the effort already spent.
Split the story into a coding task and a testing task and count only the coding task as done.
Count it as done because the code is written and the developer is confident in it.
Leave it uncounted as finished until it meets the acceptance criteria and the definition of done.
questions.why: In adaptive tracking only finished, accepted items count, so partly built work stays in the remaining total until it meets the stated conditions.

questions.prompt: A sponsor asks whether an adaptive project still matches its original plan, since the backlog has been reordered twice. Which reply fits adaptive tracking?
choices: Report the remaining backlog points and the trend in accepted points per iteration, since the plan is expected to shift.
Show planned value against earned value for the whole project to date.
Explain that the story estimates are a contract and cannot move without approval.
Compare current work against the original scope baseline and file a change request for each gap.
questions.why: Adaptive tracking asks where the work stands now using accepted points and their trend, rather than measuring conformance to an original baseline as predictive tracking does.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run predictive projects how adaptive tracking differs from predictive tracking in terms of scope inputs and progress measures, and name one limit or tradeoff of the adaptive approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: In a predictive project we agree a full scope baseline early, usually from a WBS and requirements, and we measure progress against that baseline using planned versus earned value. Changes go through change control. In an adaptive project the main scope input is a prioritized product backlog of user stories, each with acceptance criteria, and a shared definition of done. We pull work into short time-boxed iterations and track remaining work, often on a burndown chart, so the forecast updates as we learn. The tradeoff is that the final scope and total cost are less certain up front, so stakeholders need to accept reprioritizing the backlog and must agree on how much is done before the project can be called complete.
rubricPoints: Predictive scope inputs are a charter, requirements and a WBS that form a fixed baseline.
Adaptive scope inputs are a prioritized product backlog with user stories and acceptance criteria.
Predictive progress is measured against the baseline, for example with earned value and change control.
Adaptive progress is measured by remaining work and completed, accepted items in time-boxed iterations.
A real limit of adaptive tracking is less certainty about final scope or cost up front.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the difference in scope inputs and progress measures back to a teammate, including a tradeoff, is the core skill here and no listed mission teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: Adaptive projects change direction as the team learns, so they rely on a few simple records that show what has been agreed, what is actually done, and what is blocking progress. These records are called artifacts. Think of a home renovation where you revise the plan as you open the walls: you keep a shared wish list of jobs, a short list of what you are doing this week, a visible chart of how much work is left, and a log of problems waiting on someone else. Those kinds of record are how an adaptive team documents and steers its work without a fixed plan written on day one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a mobile app and its priorities change every two weeks, so there is no fixed plan written at the start. What single shared, ordered list would you expect the team to keep so everyone can see what is still left to build and which item matters most?
lessons.teach:
The main artifacts of an adaptive project are records the team uses to document work and keep it under control. The product backlog is the ordered list of everything the product may need, with the most valuable or urgent items at the top. The product owner, the person who decides priority, maintains it. The sprint backlog is the subset the team chooses for one time-boxed iteration, called a sprint, which is a fixed-length period such as two weeks. It holds the chosen items plus the team's plan for delivering them. A story point is a relative estimate of effort, used to size items against each other. The increment is the working result that exists at the end of a sprint and meets the definition of done, the shared checklist of what finished means. For control, teams use information radiators, which are visible displays of status. A burndown chart shows remaining work falling across a sprint. A burnup chart shows completed work rising against a total scope line. An impediment log records blockers the team cannot solve alone, and someone must own removing each one.

These artifacts exist because scope is expected to change. Instead of freezing a baseline, the team keeps each record current and visible. Each one answers a quick question: what is next, what are we doing now, is it done, and what is stuck.

Worked example: a sprint starts with 40 story points in the sprint backlog. On day three the team has finished 8 points, so the burndown shows 32 remaining. Halfway through, a stakeholder requests a 5-point feature. It goes into the product backlog, not the current sprint, unless the product owner and team agree to swap it in. The burndown stays honest while the product backlog grows.

Common mistake: editing the sprint backlog mid-sprint without agreement, or treating the burndown as a promise. Either hides real scope change and makes the chart look better than the work is.

Consequence: if the impediment log is ignored, blocked work sits untracked and the chart drops late, so the team learns about trouble only at the end of the sprint.

The artifacts document the work, and the control comes from keeping them current and visible.

questions.prompt: A county library team building a book-reservation feature starts a sprint with 24 story points in its sprint backlog. On day four the team has finished 9 points, so the burndown chart shows 15 points remaining. Partway through, a librarian asks for a 6-point overdue-notice feature. The product owner and the team do not agree to swap it into the current sprint. Step 3, which the learner must supply: the request is recorded in the ______, and the sprint total stays at 24 points.
choices: product backlog, which keeps the sprint backlog unchanged at 24 points
increment, because the new feature is working software that should be counted now
impediment log, because the new feature is a blocker to the reservation work
sprint backlog, which raises the sprint total to 30 points
questions.why: Requests that arrive mid-sprint go into the product backlog unless the product owner and team agree to bring them in, so the sprint backlog and its chart stay honest.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a burnup chart as used in an adaptive project?
choices: It lists blockers the team cannot solve alone, with an owner for each.
It shows completed work rising against a total scope line, so scope changes are visible.
It shows remaining work falling across a sprint toward zero.
It holds the ordered list of everything the product may need.
questions.why: A burnup chart plots completed work rising against a total scope line, which makes scope growth visible, unlike a burndown that shows remaining work falling.

questions.prompt: A testing engineer cannot start checks because a vendor must issue an access key that the team cannot obtain on its own. Which artifact should capture this, and what must be attached to it?
choices: The burndown chart, with the testing item marked as done so the chart stays accurate
The impediment log, with a named owner responsible for removing the blocker
The sprint backlog, with a story point estimate added to the testing item
The definition of done checklist, with the access key added as a required step
questions.why: Blockers the team cannot solve alone belong in the impediment log, and each entry needs someone who owns removing it.

questions.prompt: At the end of a sprint, a team's feature works, but the shared checklist of what finished means still requires a step that was not completed. How should the team treat the item's status?
choices: Done, because the feature works and the step is only paperwork
Done, because a finished item shows at zero on the burndown chart
Half done, so it counts as half a story point toward the sprint total
Not done, because the increment must meet the definition of done
questions.why: The increment is the working result that meets the definition of done, the shared checklist of what finished means, so an item missing a required step is not finished.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which artifacts you would check to learn what the team is working on this sprint, whether it is on track, and what is blocking it. Name one limit of relying on a burndown chart alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the sprint backlog, since it shows exactly which items the team committed to for this sprint. To judge whether we are on track, I would look at the burndown chart, which shows remaining work trending down toward zero by the sprint end. For blockers, I would check the impediment log, because a blocked item can sit unnoticed while the chart looks fine. The limit of the burndown is that it only counts remaining points. It cannot show whether the finished work actually meets the definition of done, and it can hide scope added or removed mid-sprint unless the backlog changes are also reviewed. So I would read the burndown alongside the sprint backlog and the impediment log rather than trust it alone.
rubricPoints: Names the sprint backlog as the record of committed work for the iteration
Explains the burndown as a view of remaining work over time, used to judge progress
Identifies the impediment log as the record for blockers and who owns them
States a real limit of the burndown, such as hiding scope change or not proving quality

suggested.rationale: That mission walks through Scrum from an operations engineer's view, the closest existing practice for using these records.

lessons.plain: Adaptive methodologies are ways of running projects in short cycles, where the team builds part of the work, checks it, and adjusts as it learns. Several named approaches exist, and they are not interchangeable. Scrum organizes work into fixed-length sprints with defined roles and meetings. Extreme Programming, or XP, focuses on how engineers write and test code. The Scaled Agile Framework, usually called SAFe, coordinates many teams working on one large product. Kanban is about making the flow of work visible and limiting how much is in progress at once. Knowing which component belongs to which approach lets you choose the right tool for a scenario instead of giving a generic 'agile' answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of twelve people builds one large product across several sub-teams and wants to plan in longer cycles that line up across all of them. Which approach do you think is designed for that coordination problem, and what clue in the scenario points you there?
lessons.teach:
Each adaptive methodology is built from named parts. Scrum is a framework built around a time-boxed iteration called a sprint, a fixed-length cycle (usually one to four weeks) that ends with a usable increment of product. Its artifacts are the product backlog, the ordered list of desired work; the sprint backlog, the items chosen for the current sprint; and the increment itself. Its roles are the product owner, who orders the backlog, the Scrum Master, who coaches the process, and the developers. Its events are sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review, and the sprint retrospective.

Extreme Programming, or XP, is mostly a set of engineering practices.
