Examples include pair programming (two people write code together at one workstation), test-driven development (writing an automated test before the code it checks), continuous integration (merging and testing code many times a day), refactoring (improving code structure without changing behavior), and small, frequent releases. Its planning uses short user stories rather than a long requirements document.

SAFe is a scaling framework for coordinating many teams on one product. Teams are grouped into an Agile Release Train, which plans together over a Program Increment, a longer cycle made of several iterations. Roles such as the Release Train Engineer handle coordination across teams.

Kanban uses a visual board with columns for workflow states. Its defining rules are work-in-progress (WIP) limits on each column and pulling new work only when capacity frees up. It does not require fixed iterations, and teams track flow measures such as cycle time (how long an item takes from start to finish) and throughput (items finished per period).

Worked example: a board has columns To Do, Building, Testing and Done, with a WIP limit of 2 on Testing. Three items are waiting for testing. Under Kanban the team does not start a new item. It clears one test, which frees a slot, and only then pulls the next item from To Do.

Common mistake: calling any short-cycle practice 'Scrum', or assuming Kanban needs sprints. Picking a sprint-based answer for a flow bottleneck adds ceremony without fixing the constraint. Naming the approach precisely is what lets you choose the correct component.

questions.prompt: A customer support group runs a Kanban board with the columns Queue, Drafting, Review and Closed. The WIP limit on Review is 3. Right now Review holds 3 tickets and 5 tickets are waiting in Queue. Someone asks the team to start drafting a new reply. The team checks the Review column first, sees it is already at its limit of 3, and so no slot is free. The next correct step is:
choices: Start drafting the new reply now so the drafting staff stay busy, then fix the Review count later.
Add a two-week sprint so the new reply can be planned into the next iteration.
Pull the next ticket from Queue only after one of the three tickets in Review moves to Closed, freeing a slot.
Move one ticket from Queue straight to Closed to lower the total number of open items.
questions.why: Under Kanban, a column's WIP limit caps how many items it can hold, and new work is pulled in only when capacity frees up, which here means a Review ticket must leave first.

questions.prompt: In Scrum, which artifact is the ordered list of desired work for the product, kept and reordered by the product owner?
choices: The increment
The product backlog
The daily scrum
The sprint backlog
questions.why: The product backlog is the ordered list of desired work that the product owner maintains; the sprint backlog is only the subset chosen for one sprint, and the daily scrum is an event rather than an artifact.

questions.prompt: A five-person engineering team at a bank wants to reduce defects in a payment module. Each developer now writes an automated test for a behavior first, watches it fail, and only then writes the code that makes it pass. Which Extreme Programming practice does this describe?
choices: Continuous integration, merging and testing code several times a day
Pair programming, two people sharing one workstation
Test-driven development, writing the automated test before the code it checks
Refactoring, improving code structure without changing behavior
questions.why: Writing an automated test before the code it checks is the defining feature of test-driven development, one of the XP engineering practices, while the other options describe different practices.

questions.prompt: A product is being built by nine teams that must plan together. The organisation groups them into one planning unit that commits to a longer cycle made of several shorter iterations, with a coordinating role handling dependencies across the teams. Which framework is this most clearly an example of, and why does it fit better than Scrum alone?
choices: Extreme Programming, because the teams use pair programming across nine groups
Scrum, because each team runs its own single sprint and the product owner handles all dependencies
Kanban, because the teams track cycle time on a shared board
Scaled Agile Framework, because it coordinates many teams through a release train over a longer program cycle with a coordinating role
questions.why: SAFe is the scaling framework designed to coordinate many teams on one product through an Agile Release Train, a longer Program Increment, and roles such as the Release Train Engineer, which a single Scrum team does not provide.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Scrum, XP, SAFe and Kanban differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing Kanban over Scrum for a team that must give predictable delivery dates.
lessons.modelAnswer: Scrum is a framework of roles, events and artifacts organized around fixed-length sprints, with a product owner ordering the backlog. XP is a set of engineering practices, such as pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration, that describe how code is written and tested. SAFe is a scaling framework that coordinates several teams on one product through an Agile Release Train and a longer Program Increment. Kanban is a flow method: a visual board, WIP limits, and pulling work when capacity frees up, with no required iterations. The tradeoff for a team that needs predictable dates is that Kanban does not commit a fixed scope to a fixed window. Forecasts come from throughput and cycle time history instead, and without a sprint there is no natural checkpoint where commitments are reviewed and reset.
rubricPoints: Scrum is defined by time-boxed sprints, defined roles, events and artifacts such as the product backlog and increment.
XP is a set of engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration.
SAFe coordinates multiple teams through a release train and a longer Program Increment.
Kanban is defined by a visual workflow board, WIP limits and pull, and does not require fixed iterations.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner work through Scrum roles and events in an operations setting, which directly reinforces the Scrum component of this objective.

lessons.plain: In an adaptive project, the team does not write every step down at the start. Instead, they keep a running list of pieces of work and decide which ones matter most right now. Two skills make that work: understanding what 'finished well' means for each piece, which is called its success criteria, and deciding the order in which to do the pieces, which is prioritizing. Think of a cook who reads the order tickets carefully and then chooses which dish to start first, based on what is needed soonest and what takes longest.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has twelve requests waiting, and the customer says 'make checkout faster.' Before you read anything else, what would you need to know before deciding which request to start first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A success criterion is a specific, testable statement of what must be true for a piece of work to count as successful. In adaptive projects these are often written as acceptance criteria: short conditions attached to a single item on the backlog. The backlog is the ordered list of work the team may do, kept by the project owner and the team together. Each condition should be checkable by someone other than the person who wrote it. 'Faster checkout' is not testable; 'the payment page loads in under two seconds for ninety-five percent of requests during a normal business day' is.

Prioritizing means ordering the backlog so the most valuable or most urgent work comes first. Common inputs are business value, risk reduction, dependencies (work that other work needs finished first), and effort. Priority is not fixed. It changes when the team learns something new, and the adaptive approach expects that re-ordering.

Worked example: a backlog holds three items. A is a search filter (high value, medium effort, no dependencies). B is a crash on the login page (high risk, small effort). C is a footer redesign (low value, medium effort). Step one: check the success criteria. B's criterion is 'no crash on login in the three supported browsers.' Step two: B blocks no other work, but a crash is a serious risk, so it goes first. Step three: A goes next because its value is high and it is independent of other items. Step four: C goes last, and the team may drop it if time runs out.

Common mistake: writing success criteria that describe activity ('work on the search feature') instead of outcomes. The team then cannot tell when an item is done, and unfinished items pile up.

Consequence in a running system: if an urgent fix sits behind a low-value feature, users keep suffering the fault while the team reports steady progress.

Priority is the team's current best judgment, and it should be revisited each time the team learns something new.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling team has three backlog items. The backlog is the ordered list of work the team may do. G is text reminders sent to patients before appointments: high value, small effort, no dependencies. I is a new insurance code table: low visible value, large effort, and H needs it. H is a monthly billing export to PDF: medium value, medium effort, and it cannot start until I is finished. All three have written, testable success criteria. Step one: H's criterion is 'the export opens and its totals match the ledger for the prior month.' Step two is missing. Step three: G goes ahead of I because G has high value and is independent. Step four: H is scheduled after I. Which statement correctly fills in step two?
choices: I is dropped because its visible value to patients is low.
H is moved to the front because it has higher value than I.
G and H are merged into one item so the team only has to order two entries.
I is placed ahead of H, because H cannot start until I is finished, even though I has low visible value.
questions.why: A dependency means H cannot begin before I is done, so I must come earlier in the backlog regardless of its low visible value.

questions.prompt: Which success criterion could someone other than its author check?
choices: The team spends the iteration on dashboard work.
The dashboard is improved significantly.
Users find the dashboard more pleasant to use.
The dashboard loads in under three seconds for 90% of requests on a weekday morning, and a tester can verify this.
questions.why: A checkable criterion has a measurable threshold and a condition a tester can verify, which the dashboard load-time statement provides while the others describe feelings or activity.

questions.prompt: A backlog holds three items. J is a security flaw that lets outsiders reach customer accounts: high risk, small effort, blocks no other work. K is a new color theme: low value, small effort. L is a bulk-upload feature: high value, large effort, no dependencies. Using the usual inputs of value, risk, dependencies and effort, what is the best order from first to last?
choices: K, J, L
L, K, J
J, L, K
L, J, K
questions.why: The security flaw is a serious risk that blocks nothing so it goes first, then the high-value independent feature, then the low-value theme, which can be dropped if time runs out.

questions.prompt: Midway through an iteration, a team learns that item P, the highest-value item, depends on item Q, which they had ranked last because it seemed minor. What is the correct response under the adaptive approach?
choices: Keep P at the top and ignore Q until the backlog is finished.
Move Q ahead of P and revisit the ordering, since priority is the team's current best judgment and changes when new facts appear.
Drop P because its dependency was not known when the backlog was ordered.
Ask the owner to rewrite P's success criterion so it no longer mentions Q.
questions.why: Priority is revisited whenever the team learns something new, and a newly found dependency means Q must come earlier so that P can actually be finished.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only worked with fixed plans how a team decides what to work on first in an adaptive project. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them that in an adaptive project, each piece of work on the backlog carries a success criterion written as something testable, so we know when it is truly done. We then order the backlog by a mix of value to users, the risk of delaying the item, and whether other items depend on it. The top item is what the team pulls next. The tradeoff is that the order is a best current judgment, not a fixed schedule. Because we re-order as we learn, stakeholders who expect a fixed end date may find the plan feels unstable, so the team has to explain that scope can shift while the criteria stay clear. Also, a poorly written criterion makes prioritization meaningless, because nobody can tell whether an item is finished.
rubricPoints: Success criteria are testable outcomes attached to each backlog item, not descriptions of activity
Prioritization weighs value, risk, dependencies and effort, and the top item is pulled next
Priority is revisited as the team learns, so the order is a current judgment rather than a fixed schedule
A named tradeoff or limit, such as shifting scope or stakeholder expectations of a fixed end date

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner work through backlog ordering and done-criteria in an operations setting, which is the core practice this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Every project has people with a stake in the outcome, and business analysis names them by role so nobody guesses who decides what. A process owner is accountable for a business process from start to finish. A process manager runs that process day to day. A product manager decides what a product should become and why. A product owner turns that direction into a prioritized list of work for the team that builds it. Roles are also sorted as internal, meaning inside the organization, or external, meaning outside it, such as customers or regulators. Think of a restaurant: the owner sets standards, the shift manager runs tonight, the menu planner decides new dishes, and the health inspector stands outside the building.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retail company wants faster approvals for customer refunds. Who would you guess is accountable for the refund process as a whole, and who decides which refund feature the development team builds first?
lessons.teach: A process owner is the person accountable for an entire business process, from the first step to the final result, including its goals and overall performance. A process manager is responsible for running that process day to day, handling its tasks, staffing, and measurements, and reporting problems upward. A product manager is responsible for the product as a whole: its market, its customers, its strategy, and its roadmap, which is the planned sequence of major capabilities over time. A product owner is a role used in agile teams. It sits closest to the development team, owns the product backlog (the ordered list of work items), decides which items come first, and accepts finished work on behalf of stakeholders. Why the split matters: each role answers a different question. The process owner asks whether the whole process achieves its purpose. The process manager asks whether it runs smoothly this week. The product manager asks whether the product is worth building. The product owner asks which item the team should build next. Worked example: a bank wants to shorten loan approvals. Step one, the process owner, a head of lending, is accountable for approval time across departments. Step two, the process manager, a team lead in the approvals office, adjusts staffing and watches the daily queue. Step three, the product owner ranks backlog items, placing a new document-upload screen ahead of a reporting dashboard. Internal stakeholders here are bank staff and sponsors; external stakeholders include borrowers and the regulator. Common mistake: treating the product owner as the boss of the whole product, or assuming the process manager can change the process's goals. Each role has a boundary. When these boundaries are unclear, requests conflict, and developers receive priorities from several people at once, which slows delivery and erodes trust in the backlog.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy wants to cut prescription refill waits from 48 hours to 12. The chief pharmacist is accountable for refill waiting time across the whole pharmacy, from the moment a patient requests a refill to the moment they collect it. A shift supervisor in the dispensing room adjusts staffing and watches the daily queue. The product owner for the new refill app ranks backlog items and places a barcode-scan check ahead of a patient-history screen. Missing step: which role asks whether the refill app is worth building for the health network's patients over the coming years, and is responsible for its market, customers, and roadmap?
choices: The product manager, because it owns the app as a whole, including its market and roadmap
The product owner, because it already ranks the app's backlog items
The process manager, because the shift supervisor runs the queue day to day
The process owner, because the chief pharmacist is accountable for the whole process
questions.why: The product manager is responsible for the product as a whole, including its market, customers, strategy and roadmap, so it is the role asking whether the app is worth building, while the other three roles each have a narrower boundary.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency is reviewing its fare-collection process from ticket purchase to the final fare check. Which role is accountable for whether this entire process achieves its purpose, including its goals and overall performance?
choices: The process owner for fare collection
The product owner who orders the fare-app backlog
The product manager who plans the fare-app roadmap
The process manager who rosters ticket inspectors
questions.why: The process owner is accountable for the whole business process and its goals, while the other roles each work at a narrower level: daily running, the product's backlog order, or the product's long-term plan.

questions.prompt: A software company's internal sales-tools team has a development team that works in short agile cycles. Finished features are ready, and someone must accept them on behalf of the sales stakeholders before they are released. Which role is responsible for this acceptance?
choices: The process owner for the quarterly sales cycle
The product manager who sets the company's pricing strategy
The product owner, who accepts finished work on behalf of stakeholders
The process manager who schedules the sales desk
questions.why: In an agile team the product owner sits closest to the developers, owns the product backlog, and accepts finished work on behalf of stakeholders, which is the acceptance role described here.

questions.prompt: A county parks department is building an online booking system for picnic shelters. A team member lists the stakeholders as: the parks staff who run the booking desk, the department's budget office, residents who book shelters, and a state environmental inspector who checks the sites. Which grouping correctly separates internal from external stakeholders?
choices: Internal: residents and the state inspector. External: parks staff and the budget office
Internal: all four, because they all work for the county
Internal: parks staff and the budget office. External: residents and the state inspector
External: all four, because the booking system faces the public
questions.why: Internal stakeholders are people inside the organisation, here parks staff and the budget office, while external stakeholders sit outside it, such as the residents who book and the state inspector who regulates the sites.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to projects how a process owner differs from a product owner, and name one limit or tradeoff of having many stakeholders trying to influence each role.
lessons.modelAnswer: A process owner is accountable for an entire business process, such as how customer refunds move from request to payment. They set the goals and judge whether the process as a whole works. A product owner works inside an agile team: they own the ordered product backlog and decide which items the developers build next, and they accept finished work. So the process owner cares about the outcome of a business flow, while the product owner cares about the sequence of product features. The tradeoff is that the product owner must balance requests from many stakeholders, and when a process owner and a product owner disagree about priority, the issue has to be escalated to someone with authority rather than left for the team to guess. Process managers sit between these roles, running the flow day to day and reporting its performance back to the owner.
rubricPoints: A process owner is accountable for a whole business process and its outcomes.
A product owner orders the product backlog and decides build priority in an agile team.
A process manager runs the process day to day, while a product manager owns product direction and roadmap.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as competing stakeholder requests or unclear escalation.
Distinguishes internal stakeholders (inside the organization) from external ones (outside it).

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining who decides what in plain words to a teammate, and no listed mission or planned engine practises that.

lessons.plain: A business analyst is the person on a project whose job is to work out what the people who will use or pay for the result actually need, and to make sure that need is written down clearly enough that builders and testers can act on it. Think of a kitchen remodel: the homeowner says 'I want more room to cook,' but the builder needs measurements, a list of appliances, and a decision on who has the final say. The business analyst sits between the people with the problem and the people building the fix, translating one into the other. Projects get expensive when nobody owns that translation, so the role exists to keep the team building the right thing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team builds exactly what the developers understood from a short kickoff meeting, and at the end the customer says it is not what they meant. Without guessing the cause, what single job would have prevented most of that gap, and who would you expect to do it?
lessons.teach: A requirement is a stated need or condition that the finished product must meet. A stakeholder is any person or group who is affected by the project or can influence it, such as users, sponsors, operators, or regulators. Business analysis is the work of drawing out requirements from stakeholders, analysing them, documenting them, and checking that they are right. A business analyst (BA) is the person who does that work, often as a dedicated role on the team. Why does the role exist? Builders and testers are experts in how to build and check software. Stakeholders are experts in what the business needs. Those two vocabularies differ, and without someone whose job is to bridge them, requirements get assumed rather than checked, and gaps surface late when changes cost the most. Worked example: a dispatch company wants a map of live vehicle positions. Step 1: the BA interviews dispatchers and asks how old a position can be before it is useless; the answer is 30 seconds. Step 2: the BA writes this as a requirement: displayed positions are no older than 30 seconds. Step 3: the BA links that requirement to the feature and to the test that will check it. Step 4: when the build is ready, the test confirms the 30-second limit is met, and the team can show it. Without step 1, developers might pick five minutes and nobody would notice until dispatchers complained. Common mistake: treating the BA as a note-taker who only records what the sponsor says. A good BA also asks what is unclear, who disagrees, and whether each requirement can actually be tested. Consequence in a running system: an unowned requirement like 'fast enough' becomes a latency target nobody agreed, so on-call engineers end up chasing alerts against a threshold that was never set.

questions.prompt: A county parks office wants online booking for picnic shelters. Step 1: the BA asks rangers how many hours before a booking starts the shelter can be resold; the answer is 48 hours. Step 2: the BA writes the requirement: a customer may cancel with a full refund up to 48 hours before the booking starts. Step 3: this step is missing. Step 4: the BA links the requirement to the cancellation feature and to a test that checks the refund cut-off. Which action fills step 3?
choices: The BA asks who disagrees and whether a test can confirm the cut-off, then revises the wording if needed.
The BA sets the cut-off to 24 hours so it matches the card processor's default, without going back to the rangers.
The BA sends the requirement straight to developers and waits for test results before reviewing it again, since the rangers already gave the number.
The BA records the cancellation feature as a separate project so it does not affect the booking team's schedule.
questions.why: Before linking a requirement to a test, a BA checks that it is right, that stakeholders agree, and that it can actually be tested, which is the missing check here.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the dedicated business analyst role on a project team?
choices: The team member who builds and tests the software so stakeholders need not be consulted.
The note-taker who writes down whatever the sponsor says in meetings and files it.
The sponsor's representative who approves budget changes for the project.
The person who draws out, analyses, documents and checks stakeholder needs.
questions.why: A BA's job is to draw out requirements from stakeholders, analyse them, document them and check they are right and testable, not to build software or simply record what is said.

questions.prompt: A project's requirements list says the portal should load quickly, with no number and no named owner. What is the most likely consequence in the running system?
choices: Testers can derive an exact pass mark from the phrase, so no BA input is needed.
The phrase is harmless because developers always pick the fastest possible target.
Nothing changes, since a vague requirement is still a valid requirement once it is written down.
Two people may build to different targets nobody agreed, and no one can show whether the portal passes.
questions.why: An unowned, untestable requirement leaves each builder or tester to assume its own threshold, so the team cannot show it is met and alerts end up checked against a limit no stakeholder set.

questions.prompt: Why does a BA link each requirement to the feature that delivers it and to the test that checks it?
choices: To give the sponsor a reason to approve the budget without reading the document.
So anyone can see which feature and which test cover each requirement, and spot gaps.
To count how many pages the requirements document has.
To let developers skip writing their own unit tests for that feature.
questions.why: This linking, often called traceability, shows whether every requirement is built and verified, so uncovered requirements become visible before the build is handed over.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks the project manager can handle requirements alone why a dedicated business analyst role exists. Name one limit or tradeoff of having a dedicated BA, such as added cost or handoff delay.
lessons.modelAnswer: The project manager's time goes to schedule, budget, risk and coordination, so detailed requirements work often gets squeezed. A dedicated business analyst focuses on eliciting what stakeholders need, documenting it, checking that it is clear and testable, and tracing it to the work that delivers it. That gives the team a shared reference when someone asks whether a feature is in scope. The tradeoff is real: a separate BA adds a role to fund and coordinate, and if the BA and developers work in separate phases, requirements can wait in a queue, so the handoff can slow delivery. In smaller or highly adaptive teams, the responsibility may be shared among the team, but someone still has to own the question of whether a requirement is actually what the business needs.
rubricPoints: Names the BA's job as eliciting, documenting and validating requirements, not just taking notes.
Explains the gap between stakeholder language and builder language that the BA bridges.
Gives one limit or tradeoff, such as added cost, coordination effort, or handoff delay.
Notes that the responsibility can be shared or adapted depending on the project's methodology.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why a dedicated role exists and what it costs, which is best practised by articulating it back rather than through a mission.

lessons.plain: A business analyst (BA) is the person who turns what people in the business need into clear requirements that the delivery team can build. Stakeholders are anyone affected by the work or able to influence it, such as customers, managers, and the people who will use the result. A communication channel is the path a message takes between people, such as a live meeting, a written document, a chat thread, a shared board, or a dashboard. Choosing the right channel means matching the message to the way people can best understand and respond to it. Good BA communication keeps everyone working from the same picture, so what gets built is what was actually wanted.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dispatch team lead needs agreement on a new rule for assigning vehicles to jobs. Three developers, a finance manager, and two dispatchers all need to weigh in, and one dispatcher has doubts about the rule. Would you send one written update, hold one live discussion, or post the rule on a shared board first? Which would you choose, and why?
lessons.teach:
A communication channel is the path a message takes between people, such as a live meeting, a video call, a written document, an email thread, a shared board, or a dashboard. The business analyst (BA) chooses channels so that requirements, questions, and decisions reach each stakeholder in a form they can use. Stakeholders differ: some need to discuss and resolve disagreement, some need to sign off, and some only need to see progress.

Why it works: different channels carry different things well. A live session lets people question and react, so it suits unclear or disputed needs. A written document is precise and stays available for reference, so it suits agreed decisions and records. A shared board or dashboard shows status at a glance, so it suits ongoing progress. Matching the channel to the purpose reduces misunderstanding.

Worked example: a change to how vehicles are assigned to jobs affects dispatchers, developers, and a finance manager. Step 1: the open question is whether dispatchers accept a rule that ignores driver hours. That is disputed, so the BA runs a short live session with the dispatchers and records the answer. Step 2: the agreed rule is written into a requirements document, so developers and the finance manager can refer to the exact wording. Step 3: progress is shown on a shared board that everyone can check without another meeting.

Common mistake: using one habitual channel for everything, such as sending every update as an email. A disputed question buried in an email often gets no real answer, and the team builds on an assumption.

Consequence: if the dispatchers' objection never reaches the developers, the rule is built as written. The team then finds out during a live shift that assignments break driver-hour limits, which means rework and lost trust across teams.

questions.prompt: A university IT team is changing the rule for how students move off a course waitlist. Step 1: the question of whether the two department heads accept a cutoff of 48 hours before term start is disputed, so the BA runs a 30-minute live call with both heads and records their answer. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: progress on the rollout across six departments is shown on a shared board that registrar staff can check at any time without a meeting. Which action fills the missing Step 2?
choices: Hold a second live call so the registrar lead can react to the rule before anything is written
Skip recording the call and rely on the two department heads remembering what was agreed
Write the agreed waitlist rule into a requirements document that the developers and the registrar lead can cite word for word
Post the agreed cutoff as a short chat message to all 200 registrar staff and move on
questions.why: An agreed decision is best carried in a precise, retrievable written document, which is what the worked pattern uses after a disputed question is resolved.

questions.prompt: Which channel is best suited to a question where two stakeholder groups still disagree and need to talk it through before anything can be decided?
choices: A written requirements document, because it is precise and stays available for reference
A progress dashboard, because it shows status at a glance
A live session, because people can question and react to each other in real time
A single email to all parties, because it creates a record of the question
questions.why: Disputed or unclear needs suit a live session because people can question and react, while the other channels are better for agreed records or ongoing status.

questions.prompt: A regional council's finance team needs to follow weekly progress on a road repair program but does not need to attend planning meetings. Which channel best fits this need?
choices: A long email thread with every update sent to the whole team
A live weekly meeting that all finance staff must attend
A shared board or dashboard that shows progress at a glance and can be checked anytime
A written decision log that is updated only when a dispute is resolved
questions.why: Ongoing progress for stakeholders who only need to see status is best served by a shared board or dashboard that can be checked without another meeting.

questions.prompt: A BA emails a disputed change to overtime caps to 12 staff members. Two weeks later, the developers build the old version because nobody answered the objection that was buried in the thread. What is the main failure?
choices: The email should have been sent to more people so that someone would respond
The BA should have written the caps into a requirements document before any discussion
The developers should have requested a dashboard earlier in the project
The team used a habitual channel for a disputed question, so the objection got no real answer and the team built on an assumption
questions.why: Using email for a disputed question buries the objection, so no real answer is reached and the team builds on an assumption, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project how you would choose between a live meeting and a written update when a requirement is changing. Name one limit or tradeoff of the channel you would not choose first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the message needs to do. If the requirement is still disputed or people need to question each other, I would use a live session, because people can push back and the BA can hear objections right away. The tradeoff is that live sessions take time from busy people and leave no record unless someone writes down the outcome. Once the answer is agreed, I would put it in a written requirement or decision log, because writing is precise and people can refer to it later, although it does not invite discussion. For ongoing status I would use a shared board so people can check progress without another meeting. The limit of written updates is that they often get read without any response, so an unanswered question can sit unnoticed. That is why I check that a disputed point has an answer before the team builds on it.
rubricPoints: Matches the channel to the purpose: discussion for disputed needs, written record for agreed decisions, shared view for status.
Names a real tradeoff of the chosen channel, such as the time cost of live sessions or weak response to written updates.
Explains why cross-team communication matters: misunderstood requirements cause rework and wrong builds.
Checks that important questions were answered rather than assuming a sent message was understood.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a channel for a stakeholder situation is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario, and no current mission covers this.

lessons.plain: A requirement is something a project must do or know to be useful to the people who will use or pay for it. Finding out what those requirements are is called requirements gathering, and there are several ways to do it: talking one-to-one with people, asking many people a set of written questions, bringing a group into one room to agree on something, writing short descriptions of what a user needs, or looking back at what went wrong last time. Each way suits a different situation. This lesson is about picking the right one for the situation you are in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bus company wants a new app so drivers can report a breakdown. You need to learn where the three dispatchers and two mechanics disagree about what the app must record. Would you send a written survey to all 400 drivers, or hold a workshop with those five people in one room? Say which you would pick and why.
lessons.teach:
A requirements-gathering technique is a method for finding out what people need from a product or change. Each technique fits a different job. A stakeholder interview is a one-to-one conversation with a person who has an interest in the outcome, called a stakeholder. It works well for deep questions with a few people, and you can follow up on answers. A survey is a set of identical written questions sent to many people. It gathers broad numbers quickly but cannot probe why people answer as they do. A workshop is a facilitated group session, led by a neutral person, where people with different views work toward shared agreement on one thing. It suits conflict. A user story is one short statement in the form: as a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit. It captures a single need in the user's own terms and is common on adaptive projects. A use case describes a step-by-step interaction between a user and a system, including alternate paths for when something goes wrong. Lessons learned is a structured review at the end of a phase or project that records what worked and what to change.

Worked example: the dispatch manager and a mechanic disagree on the fields the app needs, so you run a workshop with both and agree one list. You then need to know what 400 drivers prefer, so you send a short survey. For the rare breakdown during a school run with no phone signal, you write a use case with that alternate path. Finally the team records 'As a driver, I want to report a breakdown in two taps so dispatch knows within a minute' as a user story.

Common mistake: choosing the first technique you know, such as a survey, for a question that needs a conversation. The survey returns averages that hide the conflict, and the build starts on a wrong assumption.

Consequence in a running system: a missed alternate path in a use case shows up later as a breakdown report that silently fails when the phone has no signal.

questions.prompt: A university room-booking team is replacing its paper form. Step 1: two department heads disagree on whether bookings need approval, so the team runs a facilitated group session with both, led by a neutral facilitator, and they agree on one rule. Step 2: the team needs to know how often 2,000 students would book rooms at each time of day, so it sends a short identical-question questionnaire to all students. Step 3 is still open: three senior staff have been rejecting bookings after the fact, and the team needs to understand each person's reasons, with the ability to ask follow-up questions. Which technique fits step 3?
choices: Send a second survey to a larger group of students
Write a lessons learned review for the paper form
Write a user story for each rejected booking
Run a one-to-one stakeholder interview with those three senior staff
questions.why: A stakeholder interview is a one-to-one conversation that suits deep reasons from a few people and allows follow-up, which is exactly what the three senior staff need.

questions.prompt: Which technique captures one need in the user's own words, in the form of a role, a capability wanted, and the benefit it brings, and is common on adaptive projects?
choices: Survey
Lessons learned review
Use case
User story
questions.why: A user story is a single short statement in the form as a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit, and it is common on adaptive projects.

questions.prompt: A warehouse project sends a survey to 300 floor staff, and 80 percent say they want faster pick lists. However, the two floor leads sharply disagree about which pick-list ordering rule to adopt. What technique should the project manager use next to resolve this?
choices: A use case covering every pick-list interaction
A larger survey of the 300 staff asking about the ordering rule
A workshop led by a neutral facilitator with the floor leads, aimed at shared agreement
A lessons learned review of the last warehouse change
questions.why: A workshop is a facilitated group session that suits conflict and works toward shared agreement, whereas a survey only returns averages that hide disagreement.

questions.prompt: A team is specifying a self-service parking kiosk. They need a step-by-step record of how a customer pays by card, including what happens when the card is declined, the reader times out, or the network drops mid-payment, so developers can build each path. Which technique is most suitable?
choices: A survey of customers about payment preferences
A use case that includes the alternate paths for each failure
A stakeholder interview with the kiosk vendor only
A user story stating that the customer wants to pay quickly
questions.why: A use case describes the step-by-step interaction between user and system and includes alternate paths for when something goes wrong, which the declined and timeout cases require.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an interview, a survey, a workshop and a user story for a new feature, and name one limit of the technique you would reach for first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the question I need answered. If I need to understand one person's workflow in depth, I use an interview, because I can follow up on surprising answers. If I need to know how many people share a view, I use a survey, but it cannot tell me why. If two groups disagree, I run a workshop so they resolve it together with a neutral facilitator. Once the need is clear, I write it as a user story so the team builds from the user's own wording. The limit of an interview is that it only reflects the people I talk to, so a few interviews can miss the wider user group. I would check that sample against a survey before trusting it.
rubricPoints: Matches each technique to the kind of question it answers, such as depth, breadth, or agreement.
Names a specific limit of the chosen technique, for example a small sample or a survey that cannot explain why.
Explains that a user story captures one need in the user's own terms.
Mentions checking one technique's findings against another where stakes are high.

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a technique for a scenario is best checked by explaining the reasoning back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers business analysis.

lessons.plain: Imagine a customer asks a builder for a dozen changes: a second bathroom, a bigger kitchen window, step-free access. A project manager needs two tools to keep track of what was asked for and whether it got built. One is a traceability matrix, a table that links each requirement to where it is designed, built, and tested. The other is a product backlog, an ordered list of everything the product might need, with the most valuable items at the top. Both answer the same question: can we point to where each wanted thing lives, and is anything missing?
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks for ten features. Three months later a tester says feature seven was never built, and nobody noticed. What kind of table would have caught this earlier, and what would each row need to link to?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a statement of something the product or project must do or meet. A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) is a table in which each row is one requirement, and the columns record where that requirement goes next: the design element, the work item, the test case, and the status. Tracing means following links forward from a requirement to its delivered result, or backward from a result to the requirement that justified it. A product backlog is a different artifact: an ordered list of everything the product might need, kept by the product owner (the person who sets priorities for the product). Its top items are the most valuable and most detailed; its lower items may never be built. Each entry is called a backlog item.

Why it works: a matrix makes gaps visible. If a requirement row has no test linked, you know it is unverified before release. A backlog works by ranking, so the team always knows what comes next and what is being deferred.

Worked example: a dispatch system has three requirements. R1 says show vehicle position within 10 seconds. R2 says alert when a vehicle enters a geofence (a defined map boundary). R3 says export a daily report. Step 1: list each requirement as a row with an ID. Step 2: link R1 to the position-ingest design and to test T1. Step 3: link R2 to an alert feature, but find no test. Step 4: mark R3 as deferred. The matrix now shows that R2 is a gap to close before acceptance.

Common mistake: treating the backlog as a complete scope list. A backlog is living and ranked, so it cannot prove that every requirement was delivered. Use the matrix for that proof.

Consequence: an untraced requirement can ship untested, and the first person to discover the gap may be a dispatcher during a live shift.

questions.prompt: A clinic's check-in kiosk team is tracing backward from a deployed feature, a printed visit summary, to the requirement that justified it. Step 1: find the feature in the current build. Step 2: follow its link back to requirement K4, which says patients receive a printed visit summary before they leave. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: confirm that the row's status shows the requirement as verified. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: Rank K4 at the top of the backlog so the team builds it first.
Export the weekly visit count report, since reports always show requirement coverage.
Add a new backlog item for the printer model, since the backlog tracks what the product needs.
Follow K4's link forward to test K-T2 and confirm the test checks the printed summary.
questions.why: After tracing back from the result to its requirement, the next move is to follow that requirement's forward link to the test that verifies it, which is what the matrix is for.

questions.prompt: A product owner says the product backlog proves that every requirement was delivered, because it lists everything the product needs. What is the best response?
choices: That is correct, because a ranked backlog lists every requirement and its delivery status.
The backlog and the matrix are the same artifact, just sorted in a different order.
Only the top backlog items need proof, because lower items are never built.
The backlog is living and ranked, so it cannot prove delivery; a traceability matrix supplies that proof.
questions.why: A backlog is an ordered, changing list and cannot show whether each requirement was tested and delivered, which is the job of the matrix's links and status columns.

questions.prompt: A parking-garage app team has four requirements. P1: pay by card within 5 seconds, linked to a design element and to test P-T3. P2: open the gate for a paid ticket, linked to a design element but to no test. P3: email monthly-pass renewal reminders, with no design element and no test. P4: print a monthly usage summary, linked to a design element and to test P-T9. Before release, which rows are unverified?
choices: Only P3
P2 and P3
Only P2
Only P1
questions.why: A requirement with no test linked is unverified, and P2 and P3 have no test linked, while P1 and P4 do.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says that because a backlog item has been marked deferred, it is no longer a requirement and needs no row in the matrix. What is the best reply?
choices: Deferred means not scheduled now; the requirement still needs a row and a status so its gap or deferral stays visible.
Deferred items drop out of the matrix entirely until they are scheduled for a release.
Deferred items should be deleted from the backlog so the matrix stays accurate.
Deferral only applies to backlog items, so requirements are always built in the current release.
questions.why: Deferring work changes when it is built, not whether it is required, so the matrix keeps the row and status to show the deferral clearly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a requirements traceability matrix differs from a product backlog, and name one limit of each that you would watch for on your project.
lessons.modelAnswer: A product backlog is an ordered list of everything the product might need, kept by the product owner and reordered as priorities change. It is good for deciding what to build next, but it is not proof that a requirement was delivered, because low-ranked items may never be built and the list does not record tests. A traceability matrix does the opposite job: each requirement is a row linked to its design, work item, and test, so gaps show up before release. Its limit is upkeep. It must be kept current, and in a fast adaptive project a stale matrix can mislead more than having none. So I would use the backlog to steer priority, and use the matrix or per-item acceptance criteria to confirm delivery readiness.
rubricPoints: A product backlog is an ordered, changing list owned by the product owner and used to set priority.
A traceability matrix links each requirement to its design, work item, and test to show coverage.
The matrix reveals gaps such as untested requirements, which the backlog alone cannot prove.
Both carry a maintenance cost; a stale matrix or unrefined backlog misleads the team.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which artifact exposes a coverage gap adds the most here, and no listed mission covers requirements tracing.

lessons.plain: A product roadmap is a planning picture that shows what a product or system will deliver over time, grouped into releases. A release is one planned batch of changes shipped to users together. Think of it like a rail timetable: it shows which features are expected in which release window, and in what order, but it is not a guarantee of exact dates. A business analyst reads the roadmap against the list of needs the product must meet, to confirm that each need has a planned home and that nothing important has been dropped or put in the wrong order.
lessons.guessPrompt: A roadmap lists a customer login feature in Release 2, but a password reset feature that depends on login is listed in Release 1. What is the most likely problem, and what should you check first?
lessons.teach:
A product roadmap is a time-ordered plan showing which features or changes a product will deliver, grouped into releases. A release is one planned delivery of changes to users. A component, in this sense, is one unit of planned work, such as a feature, an enhancement, or a technical change. A requirement is a stated need the product must meet. A dependency is a component that cannot work properly until another component already exists. A theme is a broad goal that groups several components.

Why it works: the roadmap turns a long list of wanted things into a sequence. Each component should map to exactly one release, so the team and stakeholders can see what arrives when and what is still unscheduled. The business analyst's job is to read the map against the requirements. Every requirement should map to a component, every component should trace back to a requirement or goal, and a dependency should land in the same release as, or an earlier release than, the component that needs it.

Worked example. Requirements: (1) customers can log in; (2) customers can reset a forgotten password; (3) customers see order history. Roadmap: Release 1 contains login and order history; Release 2 contains password reset. Step 1: match each requirement to one component. Step 2: check dependencies. Password reset needs login, and login ships in Release 1, so Release 2 is acceptable. Step 3: check coverage. All three requirements appear exactly once. The roadmap is consistent. If password reset were moved into Release 1 while login stayed in Release 2, the plan would be inconsistent, because a feature would ship before the thing it depends on.

Common mistake: treating a roadmap's dates as firm commitments, or reading a component's release slot as proof that it is finished. A roadmap shows planned intent, and it changes as priorities shift.

Consequence: when a dependency ships late, the dependent feature can break in production. For example, a new screen may call a service that does not yet exist and show errors to users.

questions.prompt: A library app roadmap is built from three requirements: (1) members search the catalogue; (2) members place holds on checked-out books; (3) staff see an overdue list. Step 1 is done: each requirement maps to exactly one component, and the catalogue search and overdue list both sit in Release 1. Step 2 is done: placing a hold needs member accounts to exist, so the member accounts component must land in the same release as hold placement or an earlier one. Hold placement is scheduled for Release 1, but member accounts is currently in Release 2. Step 3, which you complete: in which release must member accounts be placed so the plan is consistent?
choices: Release 2, where it currently sits
Release 1, the same release as hold placement
Release 3, after the feature that needs it
Unscheduled, since it is not a user-facing feature
questions.why: A dependency must ship in the same release as, or an earlier release than, the component that needs it, and hold placement is in Release 1, so member accounts must move to Release 1.

questions.prompt: On a product roadmap, which statement correctly describes a dependency?
choices: A component that cannot work properly until another component already exists
A stated need that the product must meet
A date the team has committed to delivering
A broad goal that groups several components together
questions.why: A dependency is defined as a component that needs another component to already exist before it can work properly.

questions.prompt: A roadmap places the checkout confirmation screen in Release 2 and the payment service it calls in Release 3. What is the main risk?
choices: Stakeholders will reject the plan because the releases are not in date order
The payment service will lose its requirement and be removed from the roadmap
The screen may call a service that does not exist yet, so users can see errors in production
The screen will be counted as two components and the plan will double-report work
questions.why: The screen is a dependent component that would ship before the service it needs, so it can break in production when it calls a service that is not yet there.

questions.prompt: A component appears under both Release 1 and Release 2 on a roadmap. Which rule does this break, and why does it matter?
choices: A theme can only appear once, so the component is actually a theme
Releases must contain an equal number of components, so the map is unbalanced
Each component should map to exactly one release, so the team cannot tell when it arrives
Requirements must be listed in release order, which this roadmap ignores
questions.why: The roadmap rule is one component to one release, and a component in two releases leaves its planned arrival unclear to the team and stakeholders.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use a product roadmap to check whether every requirement is covered by a release. Name one limit of the roadmap you would keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the requirements we agreed on and finding the component on the roadmap that delivers each one. Every requirement should map to one component, and that component should sit in exactly one release. Then I would check dependencies: if a component needs another to work, the needed one must ship in the same release or an earlier one. Anything without a home in a release is a gap I would raise with the product owner, and any component with no matching requirement is a question about scope. The limit I would keep in mind is that a roadmap shows planned intent, not commitment. Release timing shifts as priorities change, so I would re-check the mapping after each planning session rather than treat the roadmap as proof that something is delivered.
rubricPoints: Maps each requirement to a specific component and its release.
Checks dependencies so a component is not released before what it needs.
Flags requirements with no release, and components with no matching requirement.
Notes that a roadmap shows planned intent that can change, not completed delivery.

suggested.rationale: Reading and interpreting a roadmap against requirements is a framework concept, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A project can be run in two broad ways. In a predictive approach, the team pins down most requirements early, plans the whole job, and then builds it in fixed phases. In an adaptive approach, the team expects requirements to change, so it delivers small pieces often and reshapes the work as it learns. The business analyst is the person who finds out what the business actually needs and makes sure that gets built. How much of that work happens up front, and how much keeps happening during delivery, depends on which approach the project chose. Knowing the difference tells you when the analyst should write a full specification and when they should keep a living, reordered list of priorities.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new app, and the customers cannot yet agree on exactly what they want. Would you have the business analyst write one complete requirements document at the start, or keep refining a short prioritized list while the team builds? Give your reason in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A predictive approach, sometimes called waterfall, front-loads the thinking. The business analyst (BA) elicits requirements, meaning draws them out of stakeholders through interviews, workshops and surveys, and records them in a requirements specification that is agreed before design starts. A requirements traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to its design element, its test case and the phase or release that delivers it, so nothing is silently dropped. Changes go through a formal change request.

An adaptive approach, such as Agile or Scrum, assumes the need will shift as people see working software. The BA keeps a product backlog, an ordered list of work items, usually written as user stories (short statements of who wants what and why). Before a story is built, the BA defines acceptance criteria, the conditions that must be true for it to count as done. Work is delivered in short time-boxed iterations, and the backlog is reordered after each one.

Worked example: a regulated city transit ticketing system with fixed legal rules. The BA runs workshops, writes a specification, and builds a traceability matrix linking each legal rule to a test. Each phase closes with a sign-off gate. Now a rider mobile app whose features are still uncertain. The BA writes stories, agrees acceptance criteria for the top five, and reviews a working version with riders every two weeks.

Common mistake: carrying the predictive habit of a frozen document into an adaptive project, so the document goes stale while the team builds to an outdated version.

Consequence: in a running project, stale requirements produce rework and delivered features that nobody asked for.

The methodology sets the shape of the BA's work: a complete traced specification when scope is fixed, and a continually refined backlog with clear acceptance criteria when scope is expected to change.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union must add an affordability check to its loan form. A regulator fixes the rules, so the business analyst (BA) uses a predictive, plan-based approach. Step 1: the BA interviews the compliance officer and writes the three rules in a requirements specification that is signed off before design starts. Step 2: the BA adds one row per rule to a requirements traceability matrix (a table linking each requirement to its design element, its test case and the release that delivers it), and links each rule to its design element. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the sign-off gate closes only when every row has a test case and a release. Which action completes step 3?
choices: The BA adds a test case for each rule to its matrix row.
The BA sends the rules straight to developers and skips the matrix to save time.
The BA replaces the specification with user stories so the team can adapt the rules as they build.
The BA reorders a product backlog by business value after each two-week iteration.
questions.why: Step 4 requires every matrix row to have a test case, so step 3 must be adding the test case for each rule, which is the predictive habit of keeping nothing silently dropped.

questions.prompt: A city parks department is building a permit-booking web tool. Leaders expect the booking screens to change after a pilot with residents. Which artifact should the BA keep as the main working list of what to build?
choices: A change request log that records every feature after it is built.
A requirements traceability matrix linking each rule to a test case.
A signed requirements specification that is frozen before any design begins.
A product backlog of ordered user stories, each with acceptance criteria.
questions.why: When the need is expected to shift, an adaptive project uses an ordered product backlog of user stories with acceptance criteria, reordered after each iteration, rather than a frozen specification.

questions.prompt: On an adaptive project, a team keeps a 60-page requirements document that is updated only at quarterly reviews. The developers build from the document every sprint. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The sign-off gate will catch the mismatch before any feature is released.
Rework and delivered features that nobody asked for, because the team builds to an outdated version.
The traceability matrix will automatically flag the stale rows before testing.
The change request process will approve every change without review.
questions.why: A document that goes stale while the team keeps building from it leads to rework and features no one currently wants, which is the known mistake of carrying a predictive habit into an adaptive project.

questions.prompt: A hospital's bed-tracking system has fixed regulatory rules and a predictive plan. Halfway through the build, a nurse manager asks for a new field for isolation status. What is the BA's first correct move?
choices: Add the field directly to the next iteration's backlog without informing anyone.
Replace the requirements specification with user stories so the change is absorbed.
Ask the developers to build the field and document it after release.
Submit a formal change request and assess which requirements, design elements and test cases it affects.
questions.why: In a predictive project, changes go through a formal change request, and the BA checks the traceability links to see what the change touches before it is approved.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how choosing an adaptive or a predictive methodology changes what the business analyst spends their time on. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would not pick for a given project.
lessons.modelAnswer: In a predictive project, the BA spends most of the early time eliciting requirements through interviews and workshops, then writes a specification and a requirements traceability matrix that links each requirement to its design, its test and its release. That matrix is what the team checks at each gate. In an adaptive project, the BA spends the time keeping a product backlog of user stories in priority order, writing acceptance criteria for the next items, and reviewing working increments with stakeholders each iteration. The tradeoff of predictive is that it is slow to respond when needs change, because every change needs a formal change request. The tradeoff of adaptive is that scope and budget are harder to fix in advance, so it is a poor match for a fixed-scope regulated contract where the whole scope must be signed off first.
rubricPoints: Predictive work front-loads elicitation and a traced specification agreed before building.
Adaptive work centers on a prioritized product backlog of user stories with acceptance criteria.
Traceability matrix links requirements to design, tests and delivery in a predictive project.
Each approach carries a named tradeoff, such as slow change handling versus harder upfront scope control.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the methodology choice back to a teammate with a tradeoff is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers BA methodology.

lessons.plain: Validating requirements through delivery means checking, at the end of the work, that what was built actually does what the people who asked for it needed. Before work starts, each requirement gets acceptance criteria: a short list of observable conditions that must be true for the requirement to count as done. A traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to the work that delivers it and the check that proves it. A backlog is an ordered list of pending work items. Delivery readiness is the judgment that everything linked to a release has passed its checks, so nothing is left unproven.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer says a feature is finished because the code is written. A stakeholder then says it does not do what they asked for. Without any further teaching, what could the team have written down earlier that would have made this disagreement easy to settle?
lessons.teach:
Acceptance criteria are the conditions a requirement must meet before anyone accepts it as delivered. Each one should be observable, so two people looking at the result would reach the same verdict. A requirement is a statement of a need, such as 'drivers can see their route'. A criterion turns that into a checkable statement, such as 'the route screen shows the next five stops in order and loads within two seconds on the standard handset'.

A traceability matrix is a table with requirements down one side and the things that realise them across the other: design items, work items, tests and releases. Its job is to expose gaps. If a requirement has no linked work or no linked test, it is not ready, however busy the team has been. A product backlog plays a similar role in adaptive work: each item carries its acceptance criteria, and an item is ready only when those criteria are demonstrably met.

Worked example. Requirement R-12: dispatchers must be able to reassign a job. Criteria: (1) reassignment is allowed only for jobs not yet started; (2) the previous driver is notified; (3) the change appears on the dispatch board within five seconds. The matrix links R-12 to work item W-40 and to tests T-88 and T-89. Before the release review, the business analyst checks each criterion against a test result. T-88 passes, but T-89 fails on the notification step. R-12 is not ready, so the release is not ready either, even though the reassignment screen works.

Common mistake: writing criteria that describe tasks, such as 'build the reassignment screen', rather than outcomes. Those can be ticked off without anyone confirming the user gets what they need.

Consequence: if readiness is judged by activity rather than against the matrix, an unproven requirement reaches production and is discovered first by the people who depend on it.

Acceptance criteria give the release decision its evidence.

questions.prompt: A library app team writes requirement R-7: members can renew a loan. The criteria are (1) a loan can be renewed once only, (2) the new due date appears in the member's account within 10 seconds, and (3) a renewal request is refused for a loan that has a pending hold. The traceability matrix links R-7 to work item W-15 and to tests T-50 and T-51. T-50 covers criterion 1 and passes. T-51 covers criterion 2 and passes. No test in the matrix covers criterion 3. Step 1 is to list the criteria. Step 2 is to match each criterion to a test result. Step 3 is missing. Which completion of Step 3 is correct?
choices: Declare R-7 ready, since every linked test passed and the untested criterion is a minor edge case.
Treat R-7 as not ready, because criterion 3 has no linked test result showing it is met.
Count the linked work items against the linked tests and accept R-7 if the two numbers match.
Confirm that the renewal screen loads, since a working screen is the release signal.
questions.why: A criterion with no linked test has no evidence behind it, so the matrix shows a gap and the requirement cannot be counted as ready.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an acceptance criterion rather than a requirement or a task?
choices: After a fine payment, the balance shows zero within 3 seconds and a receipt email shows the amount paid.
The payments developer finishes the fine module by Friday.
Build the fine-payment page for members.
Members need an easier way to deal with fines.
questions.why: It states an outcome that two observers could check with the same result, while the other options describe a task, a general need, or a schedule.

questions.prompt: A traceability matrix for a warehouse scanner app links requirement S-4 (scanners keep working offline and sync when reconnected) to design item D-3, work item W-9, and test T-14. T-14 passes its offline-capture check. The sync-on-reconnect criterion has no linked test. What does the matrix show?
choices: S-4 is ready, because it has linked design, linked work and a passing test.
S-4 is ready once the developer confirms that the sync code has been merged.
The matrix shows nothing useful until release items are linked to every requirement.
S-4 is not ready, because one criterion has no linked test and so no evidence that it is met.
questions.why: The matrix exposes gaps, and a criterion without a linked test is unproven, so the requirement is not ready regardless of other linked items.

questions.prompt: In an adaptive team, a backlog item called 'Speed up product search' has the criterion that results return in under one second with 10,000 products in the catalogue. The sprint demo ran against 200 products, and the team marks the item done. Is the item ready?
choices: Yes, the demo shows search is faster, so the item is ready.
Only after the product owner has signed off on the wording of the criterion.
Yes, because the team agreed to mark the item done at the demo.
No, the criterion is not demonstrably met at the stated scale, so the item is not ready.
questions.why: A backlog item is ready only when its acceptance criteria are demonstrably met, and a test at 200 products does not show the 10,000-product criterion is met.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how acceptance criteria and a traceability matrix together let you judge whether a release is ready, and name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Acceptance criteria say, for each requirement, which observable result counts as done. The traceability matrix links each requirement to the work that delivers it and the test that checks it. Put together, I can go down the list and see whether every requirement has a passing check against its criteria. Any requirement with no linked test, or with a failing one, means the release is not ready. The limit is that the matrix only proves what was written down. If a need was never captured as a requirement, no row exists for it, and the matrix can look complete while a real gap goes unnoticed. So I would still confirm with the stakeholders that the requirement list reflects what they need, and treat the matrix as evidence of coverage rather than proof of value.
rubricPoints: Acceptance criteria are observable, checkable conditions attached to each requirement.
A traceability matrix links requirements to work items and tests, which exposes gaps.
Readiness means every linked requirement has passing evidence against its criteria.
The approach only covers requirements that were captured, so missing needs stay invisible.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how criteria and a matrix support a release decision and where they fall short, which is best practised by saying it back.

scenarios.title: Order-Tracking System Replacement at Ferrow Bay Foods
scenarios.scenario: Ferrow Bay Foods is a fictional mid-sized packaged food company. Its daily work includes running two bottling lines and shipping orders. Operations means ongoing, repeating work that keeps the business running with no set end date. This quarter the company also has a project: replacing its aging order-tracking software with a new system. A project is a temporary effort with a defined start, a defined end, and a specific goal. The team plans to gather all requirements and get them signed off before any building starts, and to deliver in fixed phases. That is a predictive approach, meaning the plan is set early and changes are controlled. Dana Okafor, the VP of Supply Chain, is the project sponsor, the executive who approved the project and is accountable for its business value. She named Luis Medina as project manager, the person who plans, runs, and reports on the day-to-day work. Mid-project, the team hears that a regulator may change product labeling rules, which could affect the new system's reports. Luis must record that in a risk register, which is a tracked list of uncertain future events, their likelihood, and planned responses. The team also has a stakeholder register, a list of the people and groups affected by the project along with their influence and needs. The project scope statement, a written description of what is and is not included, lists 'migrate order history from the old system' but says nothing about warehouse scanners or who approves the go-live cutover, the moment the new system takes over from the old one. Complete the following: 1. Place the order-tracking replacement against operations, a program, and a portfolio, and state whether its delivery approach is predictive or adaptive, giving one reason. 2. Sort each of these three items as an issue, a risk, an assumption, or a constraint, and explain each choice in one sentence: (a) the new system must be live before the March fiscal-year audit; (b) the team is treating the warehouse scanners as compatible because the vendor has not yet confirmed it; (c) the scanner vendor has missed two delivery dates, and cutover is now blocked until the scanners arrive. 3. Identify two gaps in the scope statement and name who should hold the cutover approval decision. Then state what Luis should enter in the risk register for the possible labeling rule change, including what he should record about its likelihood and response.
subParts: Place the project against operations, program, and portfolio, and name its delivery approach with one reason.
Sort three items as issue, risk, assumption, or constraint, with one sentence of reasoning each.
Identify two scope statement gaps, name the cutover approver, and describe the risk register entry for the labeling change.
modelAnswer: This is a project, not operations, because it has a defined start and end and a specific goal of replacing the order-tracking system, while the bottling and shipping work is ongoing. It is not a program, because a program is a group of related projects managed together to reach a shared benefit, and only one project is described here. It is not a portfolio, which is the full collection of projects and programs an organization selects and funds to meet its strategy, and no portfolio-level decisions are described. The delivery approach is predictive, because requirements are gathered and signed off before building starts and work proceeds in fixed phases; the reason is that the plan is set early and changes go through control.

(a) Constraint: the March audit date is a fixed limit the project must work within, not an event that may or may not happen. (b) Assumption: the team is proceeding as if something is true without confirmation, so it is recorded as an assumption that needs checking; it becomes a risk if it proves false. (c) Issue: the missed delivery dates have already happened and are blocking cutover now, so it is a current problem that needs action, not a possible future event.

Two gaps: the scope statement does not mention the warehouse scanners, which means it is unclear whether they are in or out of scope; and it does not name who approves go-live cutover. The cutover approver should be the project sponsor, Dana Okafor, because the sponsor is accountable for business value and the go-live decision carries business risk; the project manager may recommend but should not approve alone. For the risk register, Luis should record the possible labeling rule change as a risk, with a description of how it could affect the new system's reports, an estimated likelihood (for example low, medium, or high) and impact, the owner, and a planned response such as monitoring regulator announcements and reviewing report design before the change is made.

scenarios.title: Scanner Rollout at Harrow and Pine Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Harrow and Pine Logistics runs a regional distribution center and must switch its inbound receiving to handheld barcode scanners before a customer audit on a fixed date. Priya Nair, a newly assigned project coordinator, inherits a predictive plan, meaning a plan-based approach where scope, schedule and budget are set up front and then tracked against an approved baseline (the original plan).
