The network diagram, which shows activities and the order they depend on each other, lists six activities: A Site survey, 3 days, no predecessors; B Procure scanners, 5 days, starts after A; C Write wiring plan, 2 days, starts after A; D Install wiring, 4 days, starts after C; E Install scanners, 3 days, starts after both B and D; F Test and train, 4 days, starts after E. At the end of day 10 the status report shows planned value (PV, the budgeted cost of work scheduled to be finished by that date) of 30,000, earned value (EV, the budgeted cost of work actually completed) of 24,000, and actual cost (AC, the money actually spent) of 27,000. The budget at completion (BAC, the total approved budget) is 48,000. 1. Identify the critical path (the longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the shortest possible project duration), state its total duration in days, and state how many days of float (the amount an activity can slip without delaying the finish date) activity B has. 2. Calculate the schedule variance and the cost variance at day 10, and state whether the project is ahead or behind schedule and over or under budget. 3. Priya must break the scanner rollout into a work breakdown structure (WBS, a hierarchical decomposition of total project scope into smaller pieces) and define work packages (the lowest-level units of work that have a single owner, a duration and a cost). Explain why activity D should be treated as a work package rather than as a summary element, and name two items that belong in its definition.
subParts: Critical path, total duration and float of activity B
Schedule variance and cost variance at day 10
Why activity D is a work package and what its definition needs
modelAnswer: The critical path is A, C, D, E, F. Its duration is 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 16 days. Activity B has 4 days of float. Its earliest start is day 3 and its earliest finish is day 8. Activity E cannot start until D finishes at day 12, so E's latest start is day 12 and B's latest finish is day 12. B's latest start is therefore day 7, and float = latest start minus earliest start = 7 - 3 = 4 days.

Schedule variance (SV) = EV - PV = 24,000 - 30,000 = -6,000, so the project is behind schedule. Cost variance (CV) = EV - AC = 24,000 - 27,000 = -3,000, so the project is over budget. A negative value on either measure means unfavourable performance. The schedule performance index is 24,000 / 30,000 = 0.80, and the cost performance index is 24,000 / 27,000, about 0.89, which are useful for comparing against the BAC of 48,000.

Activity D should be a work package because it is the lowest level at which the work can be given one owner, a fixed duration and a cost estimate, and tracked to a clear deliverable. A summary element only groups child items and cannot be directly assigned or measured as a unit. Two items that belong in its definition are a named owner (the person responsible for delivery) and acceptance criteria or a deliverable such as wiring installed and tested to the wiring plan from C, along with its duration of 4 days, its cost estimate and its predecessor C.

scenarios.title: Warehouse Scanner App at Harbor Lane Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Logistics is a fictional regional freight company with about 140 staff. Its operations team wants a new handheld scanner app that warehouse workers use to log pallet moves. The product owner, Dana Whitfield, has a rough list of wanted features but says the warehouse supervisors will change their minds once they try early versions. The development team is six people in one office, and Dana can attend a review with users every two weeks. A separate stream of work handles production bugs that arrive from warehouses at unpredictable times. Your role is project manager. Use the course terms in your answers. An adaptive approach is a way of working where scope is refined as the team learns, rather than fixed in full at the start. A predictive approach fixes scope, schedule, and cost early and tracks against that plan. An iteration is a fixed time-box, a short window of work that ends with something usable. A backlog is an ordered list of pending work items. Answer these: 1. Explain whether an adaptive or predictive approach fits this project better, citing at least two organizational or environmental factors. 2. The bug-fix stream has no fixed plan and arrives unpredictably. Say whether Scrum or Kanban fits that stream better, and explain why in terms of how each handles work flow and time-boxes. 3. The team's work breakdown structure, which is a hierarchical decomposition of all deliverables, has a branch called 'Pallet move logging' with five child deliverables. Show how you would turn that branch into iteration units, state one advantage and one disadvantage of your choice, and name the artifact that orders the resulting work.
subParts: Adaptive versus predictive choice with two supporting factors
Scrum versus Kanban for the unplanned bug-fix stream
Turning the WBS branch into iterations, one advantage, one disadvantage, and the ordering artifact
modelAnswer: Adaptive fits better. The requirements are uncertain because supervisors will change their minds after seeing early versions, which is a sign that scope should be refined as learning happens rather than locked up front. Two factors support this. First, the organizational environment: the team sits in one office and the product owner can join a user review every two weeks, so feedback can be frequent and close, which adaptive methods depend on. Second, the organizational process assets, meaning the company's existing templates, lessons learned, and past project records: if Harbor Lane has no history of delivering fixed-scope software on schedule, a predictive plan would rest on guesses. A common mistake is to pick a method based on the team's preference rather than on factors like how stable requirements are, how available stakeholders are, and how the organization handles change. If you lock scope under a predictive plan here, the likely consequence is a finished app that supervisors reject, with change requests piling up against a baseline that no longer matches what the business needs.

Kanban fits the bug-fix stream better. Scrum organizes work into fixed iterations, usually two to four weeks, with a planned set of items committed at the start and a review at the end. That rhythm suits planned feature work but breaks down when urgent defects arrive at random times, because a mid-iteration bug either disrupts the commitment or waits too long. Kanban is a flow method: work items sit on a visual board with columns for stages, and the team limits how many items are in progress at once (a work-in-progress limit). New defects are pulled in as capacity frees up, and no fixed time-box is required. A worked example: the board has columns To Do, In Progress, Testing, Done, and a limit of three items in progress. A new warehouse crash arrives; if three items are already in progress, the team must finish one before pulling the crash in, which keeps urgent work visible and prevents overload. A common mistake is to run bug fixes inside a Scrum sprint and then be surprised when committed feature work slips. Consequence: the feature iteration misses its goal because urgent fixes kept consuming capacity without being planned.

Take the 'Pallet move logging' branch and group its five child deliverables into logical iteration units, which are coherent slices of work that each produce something a user or reviewer can check. For example, if the five children are scan capture, location lookup, move confirmation, error messages, and offline sync, you might group scan capture with location lookup into iteration one, since a worker can then scan and see a location, and group move confirmation with error messages into iteration two. An iteration boundary is the fixed end point where that slice is reviewed and the next one is chosen. The advantage is that each iteration yields working software that supervisors can test, so their feedback can change the next slice. The disadvantage is that grouping by logical unit can leave dependencies unclear: offline sync may need pieces from earlier iterations, so the team may need extra coordination or rework. The artifact that orders the work is the product backlog, the single prioritized list of all pending items, with the top items refined and committed for the next iteration. A common mistake is to cut the WBS into equal-sized time slices regardless of what each piece delivers, which produces iterations that are not usable on their own. Consequence: at the review, nothing demonstrable is ready, so the feedback loop that justified the adaptive choice stalls.

scenarios.title: Returns Portal Requirements at Brightwater Parcels
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcels Ltd is a fictional mid-sized parcel delivery company. It is building a customer returns portal, a web page where a customer requests a return and prints a shipping label. Dana Okafor, a project manager in her first month, is leading the work. The front-end portal uses an adaptive approach, meaning short build cycles with frequent reviews. The warehouse integration uses a predictive approach, meaning a fixed plan with formal sign-off gates. Ravi, the business analyst, has reported three open issues. First, nobody has written down the refund rule for damaged goods. Second, warehouse staff at four depots must be consulted about how returns are handled today. Third, the release 1 requirements list was written six weeks ago and has never been checked against the test results. Dana must handle all three before the next steering meeting. 1. Identify which stakeholder role should own the decision on the damaged-goods refund rule, and say whether that role is internal or external to Brightwater. 2. Recommend one or two requirements-gathering techniques for learning how the four depots handle returns today, and justify your choice against the alternatives. 3. Explain how Dana would use a requirements traceability matrix to judge whether release 1 is ready for delivery, and name the specific gap she should look for.
subParts: Choose the right stakeholder role for the damaged-goods refund rule and state internal or external
Recommend a requirements-gathering technique for the four depots and justify it
Use a requirements traceability matrix to judge release 1 delivery readiness
modelAnswer: The refund rule is a business policy, so it belongs to the process owner. A process owner is the person accountable for how a whole business process performs end to end and which rules it follows; for returns, this would be the Head of Customer Returns. The process owner is an internal role because the decision sits inside Brightwater. A process manager, by contrast, runs the day-to-day steps of the process, and a product owner is the person who orders the portal's product backlog (the ranked list of work items the development team will build). A product owner sets build priority but usually does not set company policy, so asking the product owner to choose the refund rule would be the wrong route. An external role, such as a payment provider or a courier, would be a stakeholder outside the company who supplies a service the portal depends on, but it does not decide Brightwater's refund policy. The common mistake is letting the product owner decide policy; if finance later rejects the rule, the portal has to be reworked and customers may have been given wrong refund promises in the meantime.

Structured interviews with the depot leads, backed by a short survey to the wider depot staff, are the best fit. An interview is a one-to-one or small-group conversation with a set of prepared questions, which gives depth on how each depot actually handles a damaged return today. A survey is a set of written questions sent to many people, which gives breadth and can measure how often each case happens. For example, Dana could hold four 20-minute interviews with the depot leads, then send a survey with two questions about how often damaged returns arrive and which steps staff take, to about 120 staff. A workshop could agree a shared process map, but running it across four sites is costly, so a single video session could be used later to confirm the results. Use cases and user stories are documentation formats for requirements once they are known, not ways to discover them, and lessons learned is a review held after a phase has finished, so it does not fit this task. The mistake is sending only a survey and assuming the answers are complete; surveys miss the reasons behind a practice, which interviews would reveal.

A requirements traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement, given a unique ID, to its source, the backlog item or design element that builds it, the test that checks it, and its current status. Dana should check every release 1 requirement row. A requirement is ready only when it has a linked backlog item, a linked test, and a passing result against its acceptance criteria, which are the specific, testable conditions the delivered feature must meet. For example, requirement REQ-014 states that a refund is paid within 5 working days. If it links to user story US-31 and test T-88, and T-88 failed in the last run, then REQ-014 is not ready even if US-31 is marked as finished. The specific gap to look for is a requirement with no linked test, because nothing proves it works; a test with no linked requirement is also a warning sign of scope added without approval. The common mistake is counting finished user stories instead of checking each requirement against its acceptance criteria. If Dana goes live on that basis, the 5-day refund rule may be unmet at launch, which would produce customer complaints and refund backlogs in the first weeks.
